articles.title: Raleigh owner starts insolvency proceedings
articles.summary: Accell, based in the Netherlands, has owned the famous bike brand since 2012.
articles.content:
Raleigh created the famous Chopper and was once the biggest bike maker in the world

The company that owns iconic Nottingham bike manufacturer Raleigh has begun insolvency proceedings.

Accell, based in the Netherlands, bought Raleigh for $100m in 2012 but said on Wednesday it had "exhausted all the available options" and was "no longer able to meet its financial obligations".

It comes after a difficult period for Raleigh, which saw redundancies in 2024 and losses of £30m in accounts released the following year.

Jonas Nilsson, chief executive of Accell, said it was "a deeply sad and frustrating situation".

Raleigh was founded in Nottingham in 1887 and at one stage was the biggest bicycle maker in the world, employing about 8,000 people at its peak.

It stopped making bikes in the city decades ago, and in 2024 it vacated its headquarters on Church Street in Eastwood to move to new premises less than a mile away.

Announcing plans to initiate insolvency proceedings, Nilsson said Accell had worked "to restructure [its] operations and finances".

"Every realistic option for the future of the business has been tirelessly explored, and none have resulted in a solution to continue the group in its current form," he said.

"Our immediate focus is to support an orderly process, provide clarity wherever possible, and work with the relevant court-appointed administrators to preserve viable activities and employment where circumstances allow."

articles.content:
A ston Villa struggling to hold on to their World Cup stars has become something of a theme of this transfer window and off we go again as Arsenal have stepped up their interest in Ezri Konsa . The Daily Mail reports that the Premier League champions, having had a bid for the England defender rebuffed last month, are coming back with a bigger offer for Konsa, who Villa value at £60m minimum. Villa for their part are trying to nail down a £14m deal for Atlético Madrid’s Italian left-back Matteo Ruggeri .

Liverpool are looking for defensive reinforcements and could swoop for the Real Madrid centre-back Raúl Asencio . The 23-year-0ld has been told he can leave the Bernabéu and various Mr 15%s have approached Liverpool about a move, reports Teamtalk. Also on Andoni Iraola’s radar is the teenage Paris Saint-Germain winger Ibrahim Mbaye . The 18-year-old, who scored a stunning goal for Senegal against France at the World Cup, is believed to be keen on a move to Anfield.

Across the city, Everton like the cut of Alistair Johnston ’s jib and the Celtic and Canada full-back fancies a switch to the Premier League, according to the Scotsman, which reports that David Moyes and Martin O’Neill have already had a chinwag about a possible deal.

It’s all happening in Turkey. Mohamed Salah, whose arrival at Trabzonspor on Wednesday brought fans into the streets, could be joined by his old mate Darwin Núñez as the Turkish club prepare to party like it’s 2023. The Uruguayan striker has struggled since joining Al-Hilal in the Saudi Pro League last year and would be available on a free.

Elsewhere, Fenerbahce have been linked with a move, most likely on loan, for Real Madrid’s Endrick . Fiorentina and Roma have also shown interest in the Brazil forward, who was on loan at Lyon last season, but Fenerbahce reportedly fancy their chances of adding Endrick to a maverick squad that contains the likes of Nathan Aké, N’Golo Kanté and Marco Asensio.

After another summer of high-profile exits, Newcastle could do with some incomings and Football Insider reckons a bid for the Tottenham midfielder Lucas Bergvall is on the cards, though Nottingham Forest are also making eyes at the Swede. Down in west London, Fulham are eyeing up a deal for Southampton’s Northern Ireland midfielder Shea Charles , who Saints value at £30m.

Middlesbrough are set to snap up the goalkeeper Radek Vitek from Manchester United from after the clubs agreed a £14m deal. The 22-year-old Czech spent last season on loan at Bristol City, making 41 appearances, and did not feature for United’s first team but that hasn’t stopped the Reds getting a 35% sell-on clause inserted into the deal, according to Sky Sports. Boro are also about to complete a £7m deal for the Spurs centre-half Ashley Phillips .

And Hamburg are keen on bringing the Leeds defender Sebastiaan Bornauw back to the Bundesliga after a year in Yorkshire. The 27-year-old has previously played for Wolfsburg and Köln.

articles.title: Alessia Russo: ‘When you join the club, you take on a part of Arsenal and the love’
articles.summary: The honorary Gooner’s game went up a level last season. Now, the forward wants to push on for more trophies, starting with the WSL Arms hooked over the bar at the front of the bus, sunglasses on, a drink in one hand and the other pointed towards the fans as she vibed along to the music and joined in with the singing and chanting, Alessia Russo was having a blast. “I had the time of my life that day,” says the Arsenal forward of the 9km parade through the red smoke-filled streets of north London after Arsenal men’s Premier League triumph and Arsenal women’s Champions Cup success . Continue reading...
articles.content:
The honorary Gooner’s game went up a level last season. Now, the forward wants to push on for more trophies, starting with the WSL

A rms hooked over the bar at the front of the bus, sunglasses on, a drink in one hand and the other pointed towards the fans as she vibed along to the music and joined in with the singing and chanting, Alessia Russo was having a blast.

“I had the time of my life that day,” says the Arsenal forward of the 9km parade through the red smoke-filled streets of north London after Arsenal men’s Premier League triumph and Arsenal women’s Champions Cup success .

It has been a running joke among fans to refer to the 27-year-old as a “childhood Gooner”, a joke which was turbo-charged when the shirt a very small Russo was wearing in a family photo with the FA Cup was Photoshopped from a Manchester United one into an Arsenal one.

While she may not have been a childhood Gooner, she’s fast becoming an adult one.

“I came to Arsenal and I wasn’t an Arsenal fan, but since I’ve joined the club and seen the people around the place, it’s impossible to not become a part of Arsenal and to feel like I support Arsenal,” she says. “I want them to do well, I’m backing them every way, and then the parade was just one of the most amazing things I’ve ever experienced. The fans, the atmosphere, the celebrating the men winning the Prem, something that they’d worked so hard for so many years, I was just soaking it in, having fun and enjoying myself.

“It was just a really really special day. It was nice to experience it with the likes of Lotte [Wubben-Moy] and Leah [Williamson] who are proper Gooners, but I think when you come to Arsenal, and I’m speaking for myself here, you kind of take on a part of it and really start to understand and absorb their love for Arsenal. I definitely feel that and it’s really nice to feel like you’re a part of something like that.

“You pick out moments where you win trophies as the main ones that stand out within your career but that will definitely always stand out for me.”

There were faces everywhere, on every balcony, rooftop, bollard and traffic light, of all ages, races and religions. Young boys, but also, in contrast to the Arsenal parades of the 90s and noughties, so many young girls. Cultivating and supporting that fresh generation of girls interested in watching and playing the game is something Russo is incredibly passionate about.

That’s the reason she launched her own foundation earlier this year and why she helped launch the fifth year of Starling Bank’s Kick On initiative, which partners local businesses with girls teams desperately in need of sponsorship and subsidises the front of shirt sponsorship.

According to Starling – which commissioned surveys of 1,000 adult female football players, 1,010 11-17 female players, 501 small- and medium-sized business leaders and 1,092 grassroots football coaches – nearly every grassroots female football club (97%) said their team needed more funds, with opportunities for girls suffering as a result.

The survey also found that 76% of female players said they will have to drop out of their team or the sport altogether if more funding isn’t secured in the next five years and 40% of female players said their team doesn’t get the same amount of funding as male teams.

“They are quite damning statistics, which is such a shame considering the growth that we see in the women’s game,” says Russo. “Over the last five or six years, the growth has just been incredible, but there’s still work to do at the bottom to build it up.”

The risk is that women’s football loses its momentum and misses out on great players coming into the pathway.

“I always say you never want to miss out on the next Leah Williamson or Lotte Wubben-Moy, you don’t want to miss out on talented young players just because they haven’t got a local team or the team that they were at folds,” she says. “It seems like such an easy fix as teams don’t need much, but obviously it isn’t because it’s still a problem.

“I look back on all the people that I met through my grassroots journey and every single one of them played a part in my career, and I’m still friends with many of them. If local businesses can invest in one team, you never know, you might help produce a superstar who goes on to have an incredible career who will always remember you being a part of it. There’s more to it than just investment, it’s that you can really have a say in a core part of these young girls’ journeys and lives.”

With no major international women’s tournament this year, Russo has enjoyed a rare summer off, where she has had the chance to focus on these broader issues she’s passionate about, as well as getting in some much-needed rest.

“It was really important that I did have some proper downtime,” she says. “Over the last few years, the minutes and tournaments have really increased, so I needed to look after my body and get myself in a good place mentally. I shut down for about two-and-a-half weeks and just enjoyed time with friends and family, which was lovely, but by the end of it, I was ready to start exercising again, I didn’t know what to do with myself.

“I quite enjoy training on my own over the summer, you get to know your best routines and habits. I often go on holiday with my family too and train out there on the family holiday, which is nice because everyone wants to get involved. I just took time for myself too, being a normal 27-year-old girl, going on holidays. I went to the England v Panama game in New York and got to be a fan and be around that buzz of the World Cup and I had Toonie’s [England teammate Ella Toone] hen do and wedding, which was amazing”.

Russo had a standout year in 2025-26, many believe her game moved up a level for club and country. How does she reflect on it after some time off?

“I’m obviously pleased with my season for Arsenal and England from a personal point of view but, ultimately, I’ll always judge it on the trophies that we win,” she says.

“We’ve learned a lot as a team over the last couple of years at Arsenal, but are really hungry for the new season. We’ve made it quite clear that we want to do everything that we can to be the team most capable of winning the WSL and Renée [Slegers] has set the standard really high this pre-season. We’ve got seven new players that have come in, we’ve got a squad that’s raring to go, the competition in it is really high.

“So yeah, I feel happy but now I really want to continue to push on with Arsenal and England and win some trophies.”

articles.title: You be the judge: my partner confronts bad drivers. Should he stop?
articles.summary: Riya says her boyfriend has road rage, but Declan insists he never loses his temper. You decide if needs to put the brakes on his motormouth • Find out how to get a disagreement settled or become a juror Every time Declan chooses kicking off over de-escalation, he compromises our safety I don’t believe people should get away with dangerous or disrespectful driving Continue reading...
articles.content:
Riya says her boyfriend has road rage, but Declan insists he never loses his temper. You decide if needs to put the brakes on his motormouth

Every time Declan chooses kicking off over de-escalation, he compromises our safety

My boyfriend, Declan, has bad road rage. In day-to-day life he is mild-mannered. But the roads in London, where we live, seem to transform him, and he gets a kick out of being heard.

I’ve watched him go from perfectly calm to furious in seconds, and swear at people for cutting him up or for driving aggressively. Most of the time I agree that the other driver is in the wrong. But being right doesn’t make confronting strangers a sensible idea.

I grew up in London and people are insane on the roads here. But I don’t ever respond because I like to save my energy. I don’t think shouting back or getting out of the car ever helps.

As a woman of colour, I also don’t have the privilege of reacting when I’m by myself because it’s not safe, whereas Declan is a 6ft 3in white man.

When people cut us up, beep impatiently or drive as though they’re the only person that matters, it can be scary or infuriating, but Declan just goes off on one.

The worst incident happened when another driver dangerously overtook us. Declan accelerated to catch up with them at the traffic lights and shouted through the window about how reckless they’d been. The other driver got out of his car and kicked off. Thankfully, after I shouted at Declan to drive away, he did. Afterwards, I was furious – he’d turned an annoying situation into a big confrontation that could have ended badly.

Another time, after a driver flipped me off, Declan started yelling again. I know he was trying to defend me, but I don’t need defending if it means putting us both at risk. Every time Declan chooses confrontation over de-escalation, he compromises our safety over a stranger’s bad behaviour.

Declan is a great partner and we usually see eye to eye when it comes to how to handle conflict. He just has a strong sense of injustice, which seems to come out on the roads. I know he likes to be vindicated, but I’d prefer him to let it go.

I don’t believe people should get away with dangerous or disrespectful driving

Riya and I have fundamentally different approaches when it comes to driving. I don’t lose my temper for no reason, I react when people behave recklessly. Unfortunately that happens a lot in London.

I don’t believe people should get away with dangerous or disrespectful driving. Why should the person in the wrong get to drive off thinking their behaviour is acceptable?

The incident with the driver who dangerously overtook us proves my point. They could have caused a serious accident. Impatient people like that are a danger to everyone. I caught up with him at the lights because I wanted him to know he’d put lives at risk, not because I was looking for a fight. Yes, he got out of his car, but as soon as it became clear things were escalating, I drove away. If I’d wanted a confrontation, I would have got out of the car, but I didn’t want to put our lives in danger.

My frustration comes from seeing people behave selfishly and never face any consequences. I know I can’t police the roads, but I don’t think calling someone out automatically makes me irrational or angry.

The same goes for people being rude to Riya. If someone shouts abuse or makes an aggressive gesture, my instinct is to stand up for her, so why do I get called angry? I’d rather she knew I’d defend her than sit silently while someone treats her badly.

Could I express myself more calmly? Probably. I’ll admit I can get heated in the moment. I never start it or go looking for fights, but I do like to have the last word. I could be less reactive. But I think Riya overlooks the fact that I’m reacting to bad behaviour rather than causing the problems myself. There’s a difference between someone making an honest mistake and someone driving dangerously.

It’s unfair to label me as someone with road rage. I don’t drive aggressively or intimidate other motorists. I’m a careful, competent driver who gets frustrated when other people put lives at risk. Names have been changed

Putting his girlfriend at risk isn’t protecting her, and Declan’s road rage isn’t making roads safer. Every time Declan chooses kicking off over de-escalation, he compromises our safety
My boyfriend, Declan, has bad road rage. In day-to-day life he is mild-mannered. But the roads in London, where we live, seem to transform him, and he gets a kick out of being heard.

I’ve watched him go from perfectly calm to furious in seconds, and swear at people for cutting him up or for driving aggressively. Most of the time I agree that the other driver is in the wrong. But being right doesn’t make confronting strangers a sensible idea.
I grew up in London and people are insane on the roads here. But I don’t ever respond because I like to save my energy. I don’t think shouting back or getting out of the car ever helps.
As a woman of colour, I also don’t have the privilege of reacting when I’m by myself because it’s not safe, whereas Declan is a 6ft 3in white man.
When people cut us up, beep impatiently or drive as though they’re the only person that matters, it can be scary or infuriating, but Declan just goes off on one.

The worst incident happened when another driver dangerously overtook us. Declan accelerated to catch up with them at the traffic lights and shouted through the window about how reckless they’d been. The other driver got out of his car and kicked off. Thankfully, after I shouted at Declan to drive away, he did. Afterwards, I was furious – he’d turned an annoying situation into a big confrontation that could have ended badly.

The incident with the driver who dangerously overtook us proves my point. They could have caused a serious accident. Impatient people like that are a danger to everyone. articles.content:
Long days with nothing to do is the whole point of summer. Turning it into a ‘making memories’ exercise is creepy and controlling

T here are a great many things to dislike about modern parenting trends – take your pick from helicopter to snowplow to Fafo – but the least appealing, perhaps, is the temptation present in all of them to treat raising a child like an extended school project.

The latest addition is something called 18 summers , in which clingy parents count down the school holidays they have left with their children before they leave home, pre-grieving the end as they go. There is no quicker way to ruin something than by filtering it through an internet trend, but this one is particularly insidious: an invitation to inject weird notes of anxiety into what might otherwise be an unstudied thing.

Eighteen summers on the other hand is designed, like most social media trends, to make us feel as if we’re misusing our time by showing us how other, better motivated people are using theirs. This is achieved via a set of social media posts carrying the 18 summers hashtag and which, no matter where in the world the images are generated, looks like a set of adverts for Center Parcs Longleat.

There has always been something creepy about the formalisation of quotidian parts of life, and I would put the phrase “making memories” into that category. It’s the animating ethos behind 18 summers, which comes with a retail shelf full of diaries, binders and other products to ensure we document every precious moment with our children – without enjoying any of them. I’m currently in New York, ground zero of acute parenting trends, where “experiencing joy” may be tackled with the same, furrow-browed intensity as “learning Mandarin” and where parents can become so feverishly intent on “making memories” for their children that they badger them into a state of complete mania. (In this world, going for a bike ride becomes so fraught with meaning it becomes Going For A Bike Ride and you’d better hope it hits that platonic ideal).

The bigger drag behind this concept is the need to turn every last human impulse into an item on a to-do list. Do you enjoy summer while also finding it enraging and boring? Well, try holding it up against an idealised version that relies for its power on a sense of loss, fear and competition with others. The word “magical” hangs heavily over this scene, too, and, who among us needs reminding that anyone who uses the word magical more than once or twice a year is a joyless weirdo. Other phrases encountered when you browse the endless Instagram reels around 18 summers: “ultimate family formula” (sounds fun!), “three steps to deepen your relationship with your child”, and “holding sand”, which refers to how fast the time goes (although in the case of this particular scene, not fast enough).

All of this is, of course, just another form of parental overreach, a way of normalising and celebrating controlling personalities. The flipside to 18 summers is the romanticisation of our own childhoods, in which, to listen to us go on, we spent six weeks out on bikes like the kids in ET rather than, say, inside watching telly. Still, no one interfered with us much. I took my kids to a climbing wall this week – making memories! – and it was like a comedy sketch, watching parents stand at the foot of the wall directing their perfectly able kids to the top. (“Honey, put your left foot on that one diagonally – no, not that one, the one next to it; up and to the right, yep, yep. YES! Good job! You’re so good at this!” As one dad standing next to me muttered bleakly, “back-seat climbing”).

I love the summers. Even when things get frazzled towards the end, I love the sense of having nothing to do, which makes a walk to the shops with my kids something to draw out for as long as we can, rather than race through to get to the next thing. The whole point of summer is that you’re not held to account, or a schedule, or in this case, a hashtag. For a short time, we can inhabit that state hovering right on the edge of boredom that – if we don’t ruin things by overthinking – seems to go on for ever.

articles.content:
Gianni Infantino followed World Cup controversies with a widely scorned plan to let private investors in. Here’s how the game’s leaders can find a path forward

How can an organisation that runs the biggest sporting event in the world also be the one that sets the rules for the entire game? We saw the reality of such a conflict at the recent World Cup as Fifa ran roughshod over its rulebook – be it over the length of suspensions or the duration of half-time – in an attempt to generate more attention for its competition. One person with extensive knowledge of the inside workings of Fifa puts it like this: “They have shown that they will bend the rules to make them more money. This is a big conflict of interest. Not only should the commercial and the regulatory parts of Fifa be separated, but so should the development part and possibly one or two others as well.”

According to Miguel Maduro, a former chair of Fifa’s governance committee and now one of the leading critics of the organisation, the creation of different corporate entities – even if they ultimately came under its umbrella – would allow for different priorities to take hold. “There would have to be a Chinese wall between these entities and they would have to have different incentives,” he says. “Those who are seeking to maximise commercial income should not be dependent on the regulatory rules and those working on the regulatory side should not be influenced by commercial considerations.”

One insider notes that Gianni Infantino’s aborted Fifa Forward Enterprise (FFE) scheme would have created such a separation “but for completely the wrong reasons”.

The least sexy word in sport might be necessary if a new Fifa – answerable to nobody bar the courts – is to be expected to follow its new rules. “Change needs to be imposed from the outside. It won’t happen from the inside,” says Maduro. He shares the belief with other critics that it would be necessary to create a new equivalent to Wada, the global anti-doping body. It would hold sporting organisations to account on rules related to governance.

“There’s so much money swirling around in football it could easily be funded,” says one Fifa-watcher. The question is under whose auspices the new body would be created. “One way is to do something at the level of the EU,” Maduro says. “Other countries could join, perhaps the UK for example, and that could then evolve into a world sports agency that would exist to review ethical issues and compliance of the sports associations.”

In this context it is perhaps worth noting that Uefa, which is leading the protests against Infantino’s FFE plan, has in recent years been moving closer to Brussels. Meanwhile another body, the European Leagues, has called on the EU’s executive, the European Commission, to intervene over another Infantino plan: to expand the World Cup from 48 to 64 teams . The commission, it said, “should take the necessary action to protect fair competition and ensure compliance with the principles already set out by the court of justice of the EU”.

As has been proven by the FFE affair, where the whole scheme was apparently devised without the knowledge of anyone outside Infantino’s office, Fifa’s president has too much power. “The president was not supposed to control the administration, but then he began to control the administration,” Maduro says. “Then the Fifa council was supposed to control the president and be involved in the real big decisions outside the congress, and they weren’t. At the political level itself you need checks and balances.”

One suggestion on limiting executive power would be to remove the president’s power to determine funding. The governance expert Mark Pieth has an alternative proposal, one he says was once mooted by the president of Uefa, Aleksander Ceferin. It would see the heads of Fifa’s six continental confederations taking turns at being president.

“It’s not an outrageous idea,” Pieth says. “I am Swiss and it happens in my country. Seven ministers take turns being the president, but their tenure lasts one year and it’s clear who the next president is because they go around in order. The effect is nobody gets really powerful. Then you ask yourself, well, why would a Fifa president need power anyway? He’s there to organise matters.”

For campaigners looking to hold Fifa to account over the world body’s existing commitments, such as human rights, a lack of transparency over decision-making and the existing appeals process are longstanding frustrations.

Equally, what Fifa does with the money it generates and distributes to its member associations can be opaque. Nick McGeehan, the director and co-founder of the not-for-profit Fair Square, has frequently come up against the limits of transparency within Fifa. “Where are the audited accounts?” he asks.

“Fifa have a development budget that is equal to many big development agencies, but not only is there no needs analysis in terms of how that money is distributed but there is literally no evidence of any audits. Go on their website and you can find all sorts of data about what money is spent, but if you actually wanted to verify what that money is being spent on, it’s impossible.”

McGeehan notes that greater transparency would also involve engaging more with the media. “It seems like Infantino only calls a press conference once every four years,” he says. “It shows an authoritarian state-style distrust of the media and a concomitant lack of transparency.”

“Fifa is a not-for-profit organisation – the money it makes is reinvested in football.” This phrase has become something of a mantra under Infantino and following the $15bn (£11.2m) generated by this year’s World Cup , each member nation can expect to receive $8m between 2027 and 2030. But not only is there a lack of scrutiny over how the money is spent, the nature of the distribution itself is questionable.

“It’s an issue that one country, one vote is combined with giving everyone the same amount of money,” says the Fifa-watcher. “The money is distributed in proportion to votes, which is completely wrong because Montserrat and Gibraltar have very different needs to Nigeria or India. It’s amazing that he didn’t look to even try and tweak that.”

With money neither distributed according to need nor determined by strategic goals to grow participation in the game, Fifa is undermining its own aims, the critic says. “If Fifa were to be judged on results, then football is more Eurocentric now than it was 20 years ago. You can expand the World Cup, that’s easy. They claim it’s development but if you get into the nitty-gritty it can be a negative. Associations spend all their money on the men’s national team, on a European coach, and there’s nothing spent on the grassroots or technical development.”

The steady funnel of funds shared with associations big and small has kept Infantino popular with his electorate, the heads of his 211 member associations. A change in who gets a say in Fifa’s decisions might be another way to achieve more effective governance.

“When I am at a Fifa meeting and I look around the table, I see very few people who have direct experience of either playing the game, or being a coach or an executive at a club,” says one senior football figure. “I see very few people who actually understand the day-to-day of football.”

The overwhelmingly male makeup of the Fifa electorate is another fact at glaring odds with the real world, while supporters are, as ever, not invited to the party. Ashish Prashar, a political consultant who regularly engages with Fifa on the game’s social responsibilities, says: “What we need is confederations to get together and form a new entity to solidify the game with the values that serve the people. The biggest item for that entity must be fan ownership of the game. The World Cup and its surrounding events should involve the public in its decision making whether that’s fan groups, fan ambassadors or elections for fans.”

For Maduro, a change in the electorate could then unlock further progress. “Currently you have voting syndicates at Fifa, which creates a huge degree of voting control,” he says. “You need to force new mechanisms of representation, and be creative in finding solutions to bring in people that have so far been absent. If you create a diverse electorate that, by itself, will create a mechanism of checks and balances that can help to lead to better decision-making in the interests of football and all its stakeholders.”

It’s amazing that he didn’t look to even try and tweak that.”

With money neither distributed according to need nor determined by strategic goals to grow participation in the game, Fifa is undermining its own aims, the critic says. “If Fifa were to be judged on results, then football is more Eurocentric now than it was 20 years ago. You can expand the World Cup, that’s easy. They claim it’s development but if you get into the nitty-gritty it can be a negative. Associations spend all their money on the men’s national team, on a European coach, and there’s nothing spent on the grassroots or technical development.”

The steady funnel of funds shared with associations big and small has kept Infantino popular with his electorate, the heads of his 211 member associations. A change in who gets a say in Fifa’s decisions might be another way to achieve more effective governance.

“When I am at a Fifa meeting and I look around the table, I see very few people who have direct experience of either playing the game, or being a coach or an executive at a club,” says one senior football figure. “I see very few people who actually understand the day-to-day of football.”

The overwhelmingly male makeup of the Fifa electorate is another fact at glaring odds with the real world, while supporters are, as ever, not invited to the party. Ashish Prashar, a political consultant who regularly engages with Fifa on the game’s social responsibilities, says: “What we need is confederations to get together and form a new entity to solidify the game with the values that serve the people. The biggest item for that entity must be fan ownership of the game. The World Cup and its surrounding events should involve the public in its decision making whether that’s fan groups, fan ambassadors or elections for fans.”

For Maduro, a change in the electorate could then unlock further progress. “Currently you have voting syndicates at Fifa, which creates a huge degree of voting control,” he says. “You need to force new mechanisms of representation, and be creative in finding solutions to bring in people that have so far been absent. If you create a diverse electorate that, by itself, will create a mechanism of checks and balances that can help to lead to better decision-making in the interests of football and all its stakeholders.”

articles.title: AFL club Geelong under scrutiny over alleged concussion deal with player
articles.summary: Player reportedly required to assume liability for future brain trauma Secret agreement slammed by AFL Players Association The Geelong Cats have been named as the club behind a reported deal with a player – who had suffered a history of concussion – that would allow the them to keep playing if the club was protected from future liabilities. On Thursday morning, The Herald Sun first reported the arrangement without naming the club, but by the afternoon the Cats had been identified by multiple media outlets. The club has been contacted for comment. Continue reading...
articles.content:
Player reportedly required to assume liability for future brain trauma

The Geelong Cats have been named as the club behind a reported deal with a player – who had suffered a history of concussion – that would allow the them to keep playing if the club was protected from future liabilities.

On Thursday morning, The Herald Sun first reported the arrangement without naming the club, but by the afternoon the Cats had been identified by multiple media outlets. The club has been contacted for comment.

AFL Players’ Association chief executive James Gallagher said the reported deal could be in breach of both competition rules and Australian law. “The game has a duty to provide a workplace that protects the health, safety, and wellbeing of players and all clubs hold this duty as employers,” he said.

“Clubs cannot unilaterally contract out of their obligations under the CBA and standard playing contract, nor attempt to avoid their responsibilities under health and safety laws.

“Importantly, no player is permitted to return to play or train unless they have been deemed medically fit to do so. We’re in discussions with the AFL to better understand the circumstances of this case and ensure this issue isn’t replicated further at the elite level.”

The Herald Sun reported of the so-called “secret deal”, made two years ago, with a player who had suffered multiple concussions to assume legal responsibility for any on-field brain injury, adding the arrangement was cleared by the board.

Former West Coast premiership coach Adam Simpson told SEN the report shocked him.

“It’s hard to really fathom how you would get to the conclusion that this is a good thing to do, and how it goes up the chain?” he said. “I can’t see how you would accept that is the right thing to do for your son or your player.”

Geelong’s chair at the time was Craig Drummond, who has subsequently been appointed chair of the AFL Commission.

Brain health, concussion and CTE represent an existential threat for the AFL, which has taken steps in recent years to make the game safer and prevent brain injury.

A class action brought by lead plaintiff Max Rooke, a former Geelong player, has been in Victorian courts for more than two years, and now includes former Cats doctors who may be exposed to liabilities for their actions since 1985. The matter, which includes more than 100 former AFL players, is expected to go to trial next year.

This year, independent doctors watching games were given greater powers to remove a concussed player from the field. The responsibility previously fell on club doctors.

That was one recommendation made under the coronial inquest into the death of Shane Tuck in 2023. Another was to limit contact training sessions, which is set to be applied for the first time in the coming pre-season.

articles.title: Inexperienced halves pair get nod for first Wallabies Test under new coach Les Kiss
articles.summary: Lonergan and Meredith to start against Jones’s Japan Kiss makes four changes to starting XV for Osaka clash New Australian coach Les Kiss has thrown his support behind inexperienced halves pair Ryan Lonergan and Declan Meredith for his first match in charge of the Wallabies against Eddie Jones’s Japan in Osaka on Saturday. The 61-year-old is looking to improve on the foundations laid by his predecessor Joe Schmidt, who won just 12 of 31 Tests over two years. Continue reading...
articles.content:
New Australian coach Les Kiss has thrown his support behind inexperienced halves pair Ryan Lonergan and Declan Meredith for his first match in charge of the Wallabies against Eddie Jones’s Japan in Osaka on Saturday.

The 61-year-old is looking to improve on the foundations laid by his predecessor Joe Schmidt, who won just 12 of 31 Tests over two years.

Lonergan, the Brumbies No 9, was named to start in the last three of those matches, with his clubmate Meredith joining on his outside in the past two fixtures following an injury crisis.

The coach has persisted with this combination, despite the presence of rugby league returnee Carter Gordon in the squad, as well as scrumhalf Tate McDermott who will again start from the bench in his 54th Test.

Kiss said his first weeks with the players have been competitive. “Every single player in the squad has pushed hard over the last fortnight to get us to this point, making selecting the matchday 23 a real challenge for the coaches,” he said.

“The players selected now have the privilege and responsibility that comes with wearing the gold jersey and we know they’ll do everything they can to earn the support of all Australians when they take to the field in Osaka on Saturday night.”

The team is not without change, however. Prop Aidan Ross and second rower Miles Amatosero have earned their first Test starts, while Hunter Paisami comes in at inside centre to replace the injured Len Ikitau.

Ross was preferred to Angus Bell, who has started the last eight Wallabies matches but will play from the bench on Saturday. Amatosero replaces Jeremy Williams.

Wingers Harry Potter and Max Jorgensen and fullback Tom Wright retain their places in the back three. No 8 Harry Wilson will captain the side for the 24th time.

With barely more than a year until the start of the World Cup, Kiss is running out of time to develop combinations in key positions and has largely continued with the group favoured by Schmidt.

A 57-10 victory over Italy in Perth last month ended the New Zealander’s tenure on a positive note. That victory was a long time coming however, after six losses stretching back to last September.

Kiss was announced as the next Wallabies coach more than a year ago, and he has been due to take charge once his contract with Queensland expired last month.

The former rugby league winger has had a long relationship with Schmidt, going back to their time working together in Ireland.

There were only three new faces in Kiss’s first squad named in July: lock Lukhan Salakaia-Loto, prop Isaac Kailea and centre Isaac Henry. Of those, only Henry was named in the team against Japan, and may debut in gold from the substitutes bench.

Australia team : 15-Tom Wright, 14-Max Jorgensen, 13-Joseph Suaalii, ​12-Hunter Paisami, ​11-Harry Potter, 10-Declan Meredith, ​9-Ryan Lonergan, 8-Harry Wilson (captain), 7-Fraser McReight, 6-Rob ​Valetini, 5-Miles ‌Amatosero, 4-Josh ​Canham, 3-Allan ​Alaalatoa, 2-Josh Nasser, 1-Aidan Ross. Replacements : 16-Billy Pollard, 17-Angus Bell, 18-Taniela Tupou, 19-Jeremy Williams, 20-Charlie Cale, 21-Tate McDermott, 22-Ben Donaldson, 23-Isaac Henry

articles.title: Rachel Roddy’s recipe for pasta with red peppers and anchovies or goat’s cheese
articles.summary: The skins may be pesky to peel away, but the result is this velvety and vibrant, flavourful pasta dish There’s no two ways about it: charring and then peeling red, yellow or orange peppers is a messy business. Just out of the oven (if they haven’t burst while baking), roasted and blackened peppers are not unlike mini balloons; the hot juices, which have collected in the cavity, gushing out as the collapsed pepper is manoeuvred from the baking tray to the bowl. Once they have steamed under a plate, and cooled a little, the peppers might be easier to handle, but the thin scales of charred skin are still pesky to peel away, and however hard you try to flick them into the bin, they will stick to forearms and foreheads, as do the slippery white seeds. Having peeled peppers, it is not unusual to find a seed stuck to the back of my upper arm six hours later. Messy and annoying, but also worthwhile, because a strip of peeled pepper freed from its cellophane skin is a wonderful thing: fleshy with velvet texture and a deep, sweet, smoky flavour. I was taught to char peppers on the stovetop by a friend’s Greek mum, balancing them on the gas ring directly over the naked flame and turning regularly. It is sometimes hard to get them to balance and they often wobble off, but if you use a barbecue regularly, that is another option, as is the oven, and apparently the air fryer, too. Whichever method you use, the aim is flesh that is almost completely or well-patched black, and cracked like bark – a bit shocking the first time, but rest assured that the more charred they are, the redder the flesh underneath. Continue reading...
articles.content:
The skins may be pesky to peel away, but the result is this velvety and vibrant, flavourful pasta dish

T here’s no two ways about it: charring and then peeling red, yellow or orange peppers is a messy business. Just out of the oven (if they haven’t burst while baking), roasted and blackened peppers are not unlike mini balloons; the hot juices, which have collected in the cavity, gushing out as the collapsed pepper is manoeuvred from the baking tray to the bowl. Once they have steamed under a plate, and cooled a little, the peppers might be easier to handle, but the thin scales of charred skin are still pesky to peel away, and however hard you try to flick them into the bin, they will stick to forearms and foreheads, as do the slippery white seeds. Having peeled peppers, it is not unusual to find a seed stuck to the back of my upper arm six hours later. Messy and annoying, but also worthwhile, because a strip of peeled pepper freed from its cellophane skin is a wonderful thing: fleshy with velvet texture and a deep, sweet, smoky flavour.

I was taught to char peppers on the stovetop by a friend’s Greek mum, balancing them on the gas ring directly over the naked flame and turning regularly. It is sometimes hard to get them to balance and they often wobble off, but if you use a barbecue regularly, that is another option, as is the oven, and apparently the air fryer, too. Whichever method you use, the aim is flesh that is almost completely or well-patched black, and cracked like bark – a bit shocking the first time, but rest assured that the more charred they are, the redder the flesh underneath.

Thick strips of tricolour peppers dressed with olive oil, red-wine vinegar and a little of the juice that gushed from the cavity (and hopefully caught in a bowl) are gorgeous just so, or topped with anchovy fillets and black olives, or crumbled feta, as a side dish. They also make a good topping for rounds of toast spread with goat’s cheese or mashed beans, alternatively, they can be paired with pasta, an idea borrowed from Ottavio Cavalcanti’s La Cucina Calabrese and Elizabeth David. I like to blend a third of the peppers into a cream, while ripping the rest into strips, short and slim enough to mix and cling to the pasta (most shapes work). You then have two options for additions: anchovy fillets or crumbled goat’s cheese, neither of which are messy or annoying.

4 red peppers, or a mix of red and yellow Olive oil 2 garlic cloves, peeled; 1 left whole, 1 minced 1 small fresh or dr ied red chilli 300g tomatoes, peeled (plunge into boiling water for three minutes, then into cold water), or tinned 4-6 anchovies (optional) 450-500g pasta (fusilli, penne, radiatori, mezze maniche) Basil 1 round goat’s cheese (optional)

Put the peppers on a baking tray and in a 200C (180C fan)/390F/gas 6 oven for 30-40 minutes, turning them once or twice, or until they are charred all over and starting to collapse. Carefully lift the peppers into a bowl and cover with a plate for 20 minutes, so they steam and cool enough to handle. Working over the bowl to catch the juices, rub the charred skin from the peppers and tear into thick strips, brushing away the seeds and pith. Put the clean strips on a plate.

Take a third of the pepper strips and, working in a food processor, blend them until smooth, seasoning with a little salt. Tear the remaining peppers into small strips that will toss well with pasta.

In a large flying pan, warm five tablespoons of olive oil with the whole garlic clove and chilli. Once the garlic is fragrant, add the tomatoes and cook for about 12-15 minutes, pressing down with the back of a spoon to break them up into a sauce. Add the anchovies, if you are including them, stirring so they break up in the sauce.

Bring a large pan of water to the boil, salt it, and cook the pasta according to the packet instructions. Add the pepper strips to the tomatoes, along with the minced garlic, stir, then add the blended peppers.

When the pasta is al dente, lift from the water into the sauce and stir vigorously, along with a handful of basil and the crumbled goat’s cheese, if you are adding it.

articles.title: ‘I’m not spying’: how Meta’s smartglasses have divided opinion
articles.summary: While some users say the wearables have changed their lives, critics voice fears over safety and privacy With more than 7m pairs reportedly sold in 2025, Meta’s Ray-Ban smartglasses are fast becoming one of the world’s most popular gadgets. While supporters say they are transforming photography and accessibility, critics have raised concerns about nonconsensual filming, privacy and data collection. Continue reading...
articles.content:
While some users say the wearables have changed their lives, critics voice fears over safety and privacy

With more than 7m pairs reportedly sold in 2025, Meta’s Ray-Ban smartglasses are fast becoming one of the world’s most popular gadgets.

While supporters say they are transforming photography and accessibility, critics have raised concerns about nonconsensual filming, privacy and data collection.

We spoke to users, and people who refuse to wear them, about the impact the glasses have had.

Based in The Hague in the Netherlands, Servaas wears his Meta glasses every day. He bought them for the built-in camera rather than the AI features and uses them to photograph and film walks and bike rides. “It’s an immersive experience,” he says. “I love everything tech and have done my whole life.”

He says the discreet camera means most people don’t realise he is wearing smartglasses, although he was once stopped by security at an event held in a government building because staff feared he might be recording. “For some reason, security didn’t understand. They were very scared of them [the glasses]. People said I should have expected that but I didn’t agree with them because it’s not like I’m spying.”

Despite allegations that Meta workers in Kenya viewed private footage recorded on the glasses , Servaas was not put off by the scandal. “I know Meta loves your data [but] I’m not worried about my privacy because I’ve only used them to record outside.”

For others, however, the glasses offer far more than convenience. Nikki, 59, from Devon in the UK, has been blind since birth owing to an inherited retinal disease and describes the glasses, which she received as a Christmas present in 2024, as “a real gamechanger”.

“I live in quite a rural location,” she says. “I could hear something going on ahead of me as I was walking down to the village shop. I said: ‘Hey Meta, look and tell me what’s in front of me.’ It told me there was a van unloading scaffolding. It’s things like that that I find absolutely amazing.”

While she understands concerns about privacy, Nikki worries public criticism could make the technology less accessible for people who genuinely rely on it. “What about dashcams? What about camera doorbells? What about action cameras like GoPros? People don’t complain about them,” she says. “I kind of worry that if people start going on about privacy and safety, it will be harder for those of us who genuinely benefit from the glasses.”

Yet the accessibility features have not transformed everyone’s experience. Karen Walter, 84, from San Diego, who has been living with severe hearing loss for more than 20 years, bought the glasses solely for their live-caption feature.

“Even with state-of-the-art hearing aids, I have a great deal of difficulty understanding what people are saying unless the person is very close to me and speaking directly to me,” she says. “I expected [the glasses] would be a great help in noisy environments and when I was trying to keep up with conversations involving more than two people.”

The live captions worked well during a demonstration in a quiet Best Buy store, she says, when she was “with one staffer who was directly in front of me, about two feet away”. However, she says they failed to perform in the situations for which she had bought them: “I have tried the glasses when in a group of three up to a group of seven and the caption feature just doesn’t work. There were too many people talking and too much surrounding noise.”

Not everyone is convinced the technology belongs in everyday life at all. Kiki, from the West Midlands in the UK, says she finds the idea of discreet cameras built into ordinary eyewear “pervasive”, particularly for women and children.

“If you try to take a picture with your phone, at least it’s pretty obvious,” she says. “With the glasses, you have no choice, as the camera is much harder to spot.”

Kiki says seeing people wearing the glasses in public has left her feeling uneasy.

“When someone’s just looking at you through their glasses, it worries me,” she says. “I imagine taking images secretly is far easier [than on phones]. You could just pretend to adjust your hair or cap, and press the button in a passing gesture. I’ve seen people wearing them. I saw someone wearing them in a cafe and just moved away because I felt uncomfortable.”

Although she accepts the technology could have genuine benefits, Kiki says her concern is more about the lack of safeguards. “For accessibility, absolutely,” she says. “But what bothers me is regulations often lag so far behind technology.”

“They have made me much more wary in public,” she says. “I can, however, see that people working in a shop late at night by themselves might feel safer being able to take a picture of someone harassing them.”

Pete, 44, from Northampton, believes the glasses point to a broader problem: AI-powered wearables collecting ever more personal data with too little scrutiny or regulation. “I’m not an old man shaking my fist at the clouds,” he says. “I’ve been onboard with technological advancement all my life, but with AI and Meta glasses, I’m drawing the line.”

He is more concerned about where the data ends up than covert filming. “I don’t know who’s getting the pictures at the end and what they’re doing with them,” he says. “Whether they’re not doing anything or they’re selling it to someone, and then what those people are doing with it.”

While Pete acknowledges the glasses could be transformative for blind people and other disabled users, he believes stronger safeguards are needed before they become commonplace. “I would like things like this to be of benefit to us,” he says. “I just don’t trust it.”

articles.title: Players hit out at A-Leagues’ conduct over pay offer: ‘Continues to erode trust’
articles.summary: Latest deal taken to media just hours after it was sent to PFA Still no agreement in place two months before season starts A-League officials have been accused of negotiating in bad faith by speaking to the media within hours of their latest pay offer, as the players’ union said the conduct “continues to erode … trust”. The men’s and women’s competitions remain without a bargaining agreement two months before the start of the new season. Negotiations have stalled recently and the possibility of strike action has been raised . Continue reading...
articles.content:
A-League officials have been accused of negotiating in bad faith by speaking to the media within hours of their latest pay offer, as the players’ union said the conduct “continues to erode … trust”.

The men’s and women’s competitions remain without a bargaining agreement two months before the start of the new season. Negotiations have stalled recently and the possibility of strike action has been raised .

The Australian Professional Leagues (APL), which operates the A-Leagues, sent their latest offer to players on Wednesday, calling a late afternoon press conference at short notice soon afterwards.

The offer invited players’ union Professional Footballers Australia (PFA) to come back to the table to discuss an updated position, which included an increase to the A-League Women salary cap.

The new one-year, bridging deal proposed also promised to commit to “setting a pathway to full-time professionalism for ALW players, with the aim of having a mutually-agreed plan in place within 12 months”.

A fully professional A-League Women competition has been one of the key goals for players in this round of bargaining, despite financial challenges at the APL and some clubs.

APL chief executive, Steve Rosich, said they were committed to negotiations “in good faith” since they began eight months ago.

“Our updated proposal underlines a real and genuine intent on the APL’s part to arrive at an outcome that both meets the near-term priorities in a responsible and viable way, and to turn our focus with the PFA on building meaningful and sustainable growth that will be good for everyone involved in the professional game,” he said.

PFA chief executive Beau Busch issued a response on Wednesday evening, criticising the decision for the APL to go to media so soon after sharing their updated proposal.

“Rather than allowing the players a reasonable opportunity to fully consider it, the APL has instead immediately announced it in the media, revealing a fundamental misunderstanding of how good faith bargaining works.

“The players deserve the respect of hearing directly about proposals that affect their careers through a genuine process, rather than reading about them in the media.

“The players overwhelmingly rejected the APL’s previous final offer due to a fundamental lack of trust that it would have secured the leagues’ futures after years of mismanagement. The APL’s conduct continues to erode that trust.”

Rosich defended the decision to go to the media when talking with journalists on Wednesday afternoon. “We’ve been silent, obviously, in the marketplace until now, but we think now’s the right time to outline where we’re at and where we’re going,” he said.

“I have spoken to Beau today, we have issued a detailed letter to Beau, he has that information. I explained we were going to articulate our position in the marketplace so the marketplace was informed – not just the players but the clubs – and we think stakeholders in our game need to know what we’re putting forward.”

The A-League Men season begins on 16 October, with the women’s competition kicking off the following day.

articles.title: Delvene Cockatoo-Collins wins National Indigenous Fashion award for textiles harvested on Country
articles.summary: The Quandamooka artist was one of seven commended for garments that serve as living archives of kinship and memory A Quandamooka artist whose work is made with locally harvested materials, Delvene Cockatoo-Collins, has been awarded fashion designer of the year at the seventh annual National Indigenous Fashion awards (Nifas). Cockatoo-Collins reflected on the core of her practice: “Take only what you need.” Continue reading...
articles.content:
The Quandamooka artist was one of seven commended for garments that serve as living archives of kinship and memory

A Quandamooka artist whose work is made with locally harvested materials, Delvene Cockatoo-Collins, has been awarded fashion designer of the year at the seventh annual National Indigenous Fashion awards (Nifas).

Cockatoo-Collins reflected on the core of her practice: “Take only what you need.”

Speaking at the Wednesday evening ceremony, she said she is guided by a story passed down through the Nunukul, Ngugi and Goenpul peoples of Minjerribah (North Stradbroke Island), published by her grandmother in 1974.

In the story, two people gather too much native honey, without thought for their community. After falling asleep on the beach, the high tide sweeps them into the ocean, transforming them into dugongs.

“That story … is just as powerful now, especially in this time of overconsumption and fast fashion,” Cockatoo-Collins said during her acceptance speech. “We are the answer to that.”

Working from her studio on Minjerribah, Cockatoo-Collins files down shells into pearlescent adornments, hand dyes and screen prints fabrics.

Some of her work “exaggerates” fine mat-weaving techniques learned from her mother, highlighting their significance. Her three sons gather and process local plant fibres, such as tulipwood and cotton tree, keeping batch sizes.

“I know that what I’m doing at home on Country, I couldn’t do anywhere else,” Cockatoo-Collins told Guardian Australia before the ceremony began at Darwin’s Deckchair Cinema.

Looking across the Nifa’s gathering crowd, her eyes light up as recognises an attendee wearing one of her black and white jumpsuits.

“She bought that in 2024 … it’s based on my grandmother’s basket that’s about 120 years old,” Cockatoo-Collins said. “I look at each piece and I know that I’m still part of that.”

“An artist I adore, Judy Watson, talked about how the DNA of our old people is in those old objects in museums … It’s the same as what we are making today.”

Cockatoo-Collins was one of seven makers recognised across categories spanning fashion, traditional adornment, textile design and business.

Throughout the night, garments served as living archives of kinship and memory.

Wiradjuri, Yorta Yorta and Gangalu designer Lillardia Briggs-Houston won the textile design award, with an entry featuring hand-turned silk, bush-dyed using river red gum, collected from her daughter’s birthing tree.

Achieving the texture of tree bark required 12 separate dye batches. Briggs-Houston said the embellished cording evokes the memory of walking on Country with her grandfather and watching his hand trace a tree trunk.

“There’s a huge legacy behind First Nations fashion that hasn’t been highlighted for a long time,” Briggs-Houston said in her acceptance speech. She traced her textile roots to her grandmother, who sewed during the “servitude era” before becoming a teacher in the 1960s. “Fashion and textiles can be used as a catalyst for change. Being able to create these garments reflects the storytelling embedded in us and that legacy that connects with Country.”

Yuwaalaraay designer Lucy Simpson won the wearable art award with a glass river-mussel shell necklace. It was made in response to grief she felt walking the dry bed of the Murray-Darling River during severe drought in 2009.

“I felt it deeply, it was a great sense of loss,” Simpson said in a pre-recorded video at the ceremony. “To see the deepest part of the river completely dry and over 2 million of our freshwater river mussels … perished in that period.

“As a freshwater woman, I have no right to say I belong to a place unless I’m giving back. The idea is to create something beautiful that can gently tell a story we have a responsibility to tell.”

Fashion designer award: Delvene Cockatoo-Collins – Goompi/Dunwich, Quandamooka Country, QLD

Business achievement award: KAFTA (Kimberley Aboriginal Fashion Textiles Art) – Rubibi/Broome, Yawuru Country, WA

Traditional adornment award: Michelle Pulatuwayu Woody Minnapinni – Wulirankuwu, Milikapiti, Tiwi Islands, NT

Cecilia Cubillo young achiever award: Jake Powers – Walmanyjun/Cable Beach, Broome, Yawuru Country, WA

Community collaboration: Bábbarra Women’s Centre x Tharangini Studio – Maningrida, Kunibidji Country, NT

articles.title: Fifa insists Gianni Infantino will remain president after Rabat crisis meeting
articles.summary: Statement reveals Infantino wrote apologies to members Infantino sorry for failing to consult on World Cup sell-off Fifa on Wednesday night confirmed that Gianni Infantino will remain as president after a meeting of its senior executives in Rabat. In a statement which also revealed that Infantino has sent written apologies to the Fifa council and the 211 member associations for failing to consult them over the World Cup sell-off, the world governing body said that he retains the full support of his leadership team. Continue reading...
articles.content:
Fifa on Wednesday night confirmed that Gianni Infantino will remain as president after a meeting of its senior executives in Rabat.

In a statement which also revealed that Infantino has sent written apologies to the Fifa council and the 211 member associations for failing to consult them over the World Cup sell-off, the world governing body said that he retains the full support of his leadership team.

Infantino had spent the day in talks with Fifa’s general secretary, Mattias Grafström, and chief legal officer, Emilio García Silvero, during which he expressed his determination to stay on in the face of mounting criticism from Uefa and the North American confederation Concacaf, both of which have called for a review of Fifa’s governance.

In another indication that he plans to carry on as before, Infantino will fly to Colombia on Thursday to attend the inauguration of the country’s new president, Abelardo de la Espriella, in the city of Cali.

“Following a meeting in Rabat, Morocco, the Fifa secretary general and members of the Fifa management board in attendance reaffirmed their full support for Fifa president Gianni Infantino, as the only official elected by the 211 Fifa member associations,” Fifa said in a statement. “In turn, the Fifa president reiterated his full support for the Fifa secretary general and the Fifa administration for their necessary and outstanding work in the delivery of his vision.

“It was discussed and agreed that the processes, communications and interactions between the Fifa president, the Fifa secretary general and the Fifa management board that support the delivery of this vision can and should always be continuously improved in terms of their effectiveness and efficiency.

“In this regard, Fifa’s top management is fully confident that the outcomes of today’s meeting will strengthen Fifa’s governance, help restore confidence in the organisation and enable us to prepare for the major events and challenges ahead in a united and transparent manner while continuing our mission to develop the game around the world.”

While acknowledging that Infantino has apologised for his role in the abandoned Fifa Forward Enterprise proposal, which would have seen 21% of Fifa’s commercial rights sold to private investors, the statement also insisted that Fifa will not tolerate further criticisms of its governance.

Uefa is unlikely to be cowed however, with the European governing body continuing to search for a candidate to stand against Infantino in the presidential election next March, which will also take place in Rabat.

“Mistakes made were acknowledged,” the statement continued. “It was agreed that it was not the intention for the Fifa council and Fifa member associations to feel excluded from the process and that the process should have been handled differently. It was further acknowledged that errors were also made after the proposal was leaked to media.

“In a separate letter to the Fifa council and Fifa member associations, an apology was made for these errors together with a commitment to ensure they do not happen again. A review will now be conducted, and a report will be presented to the Fifa council at its next scheduled meeting.

“As previously communicated, the FFE proposal, which would have been subject to the approval of the Fifa member associations and the Fifa council, is now off the table. With the project withdrawn, it was agreed that Fifa will no longer tolerate any attacks on its integrity, good governance and due process and will take all necessary measures to protect and safeguard its name and reputation.

“There are always lessons to be learned, and Fifa will continue to improve its processes in light of this experience. In this instance, however, it is important to stress that, although mistakes were made, everything that was done was done in full compliance with the Fifa regulatory framework.

“Fifa will work closely with the relevant stakeholders to examine how it can further support the development of the game through the Fifa Forward programme for the benefit of Fifa’s 211 member associations, the confederations and the regional associations.”

Infantino and Grafström appeared together at the Malawi v Zambia Women’s Africa Cup of Nations group game on Wednesday as a show of solidarity, having also written a jointly signed letter to Fifa council members and vice-presidents echoing the Fifa statement.

In a statement which also revealed that Infantino has sent written apologies to the Fifa council and the 211 member associations for failing to consult them over the World Cup sell-off, the world governing body said that he retains the full support of his leadership team.

Infantino had spent the day in talks with Fifa’s general secretary, Mattias Grafström, and chief legal officer, Emilio García Silvero, during which he expressed his determination to stay on in the face of mounting criticism from Uefa and the North American confederation Concacaf, both of which have called for a review of Fifa’s governance.

In another indication that he plans to carry on as before, Infantino will fly to Colombia on Thursday to attend the inauguration of the country’s new president, Abelardo de la Espriella, in the city of Cali.

“Following a meeting in Rabat, Morocco, the Fifa secretary general and members of the Fifa management board in attendance reaffirmed their full support for Fifa president Gianni Infantino, as the only official elected by the 211 Fifa member associations,” Fifa said in a statement. “In turn, the Fifa president reiterated his full support for the Fifa secretary general and the Fifa administration for their necessary and outstanding work in the delivery of his vision.

“It was discussed and agreed that the processes, communications and interactions between the Fifa president, the Fifa secretary general and the Fifa management board that support the delivery of this vision can and should always be continuously improved in terms of their effectiveness and efficiency.

“In this regard, Fifa’s top management is fully confident that the outcomes of today’s meeting will strengthen Fifa’s governance, help restore confidence in the organisation and enable us to prepare for the major events and challenges ahead in a united and transparent manner while continuing our mission to develop the game around the world.”

While acknowledging that Infantino has apologised for his role in the abandoned Fifa Forward Enterprise proposal, which would have seen 21% of Fifa’s commercial rights sold to private investors, the statement also insisted that Fifa will not tolerate further criticisms of its governance.

Uefa is unlikely to be cowed however, with the European governing body continuing to search for a candidate to stand against Infantino in the presidential election next March, which will also take place in Rabat.

“Mistakes made were acknowledged,” the statement continued. “It was agreed that it was not the intention for the Fifa council and Fifa member associations to feel excluded from the process and that the process should have been handled differently. It was further acknowledged that errors were also made after the proposal was leaked to media.

“In a separate letter to the Fifa council and Fifa member associations, an apology was made for these errors together with a commitment to ensure they do not happen again. A review will now be conducted, and a report will be presented to the Fifa council at its next scheduled meeting.

“As previously communicated, the FFE proposal, which would have been subject to the approval of the Fifa member associations and the Fifa council, is now off the table. With the project withdrawn, it was agreed that Fifa will no longer tolerate any attacks on its integrity, good governance and due process and will take all necessary measures to protect and safeguard its name and reputation.

“There are always lessons to be learned, and Fifa will continue to improve its processes in light of this experience. In this instance, however, it is important to stress that, although mistakes were made, everything that was done was done in full compliance with the Fifa regulatory framework.

“Fifa will work closely with the relevant stakeholders to examine how it can further support the development of the game through the Fifa Forward programme for the benefit of Fifa’s 211 member associations, the confederations and the regional associations.”

Infantino and Grafström appeared together at the Malawi v Zambia Women’s Africa Cup of Nations group game on Wednesday as a show of solidarity, having also written a jointly signed letter to Fifa council members and vice-presidents echoing the Fifa statement.

articles.title: Mykhailo Mudryk returns in Chelsea defeat as Real Betis see off Arsenal
articles.summary: Chelsea beaten 1-0 by Juventus in Hong Kong friendly Arsenal defeated 3-1 by Real Betis in Dublin Xabi Alonso hailed Mykhailo Mudryk’s “emotional” return from a doping ban as the winger played for Chelsea for the first time in nearly two years in a 1-0 friendly defeat by Juventus in Hong Kong on Wednesday. Mudryk came on as a substitute for Nicolas Jackson in the 82nd minute, drawing applause from his teammates and loud cheers from Chelsea fans in the 43,575 crowd at Kai Tak Sports Park. Continue reading...
articles.content:
Xabi Alonso hailed Mykhailo Mudryk’s “emotional” return from a doping ban as the winger played for Chelsea for the first time in nearly two years in a 1-0 friendly defeat by Juventus in Hong Kong on Wednesday.

Mudryk came on as a substitute for Nicolas Jackson in the 82nd minute, drawing applause from his teammates and loud cheers from Chelsea fans in the 43,575 crowd at Kai Tak Sports Park.

The Ukraine international has not played a competitive match since November 2024, having been provisionally suspended after returning an “adverse finding” for the banned substance meldonium.

However, the 25-year-old was cleared to return to action after resolving the case with the Football Association. Despite a lively cameo on the left side, Mudryk was unable to stop Juventus taking the spoils courtesy of a wonderful second-half strike from the Kosovo international Edon Zhegrova.

“Really pleased for him. It was emotional for everyone from the club to see him back,” Alonso said of Mudryk.

Arsenal were punished for defensive errors as they slipped to a 3-1 friendly defeat by Real Betis at the Aviva Stadium in Dublin.

The Premier League champions fell behind to first-half goals from Rodrigo Riquelme and Nelson Deossa and although the Gunners hit back through Piero Hincapié, Pablo Fornals struck a third for Betis before the break. Mikel Arteta named an unchanged lineup after his side won Saturday’s opening friendly match 4-1 in Spain against Girona, but they fell behind in the ninth minute when goalkeeper Kepa Arrizabalaga failed to make contact with a corner and Riquelme lashed home at the back post.

Christos Tzolis failed to take advantage for Arsenal when Betis goalkeeper Álvaro Valles passed the ball straight to the Gunners’ summer signing before Deossa put the visitors 2-0 up with a 30-yard thunderbolt into the top corner.

Arsenal reduced the deficit when Valles misjudged a corner from Tzolis for Hincapié to head home, but Betis restored their two-goal advantage before the break as former West Ham midfielder Fornals swept the ball beyond a stationary Arrizabalaga following Kai Havertz’s misplaced pass.

Arteta made wholesale changes at half-time, with the 16-year-old Marli Salmon appearing at centre-half, and neither side created a clearcut scoring chance as the game lost its momentum.

articles.title: Marmots facing money troubles turn to OnlyFans
articles.summary: A Colorado lab researching the ground-squirrels comes up with an innovative way to raise money after funding cuts.
articles.content:
Marmots - chubby, ground-dwelling squirrels - are the latest stars on the adult platform OnlyFans.

That's thanks to the efforts of Colorado-based biologist Dr Daniel Blumstein, the head of a long-running field study on marmots, who was worried about its financial future after federal funding to universities was cut.

Blumstein told the BBC he recently launched an account on OnlyFans, which is known mostly for sexually explicit content, and began posting "uncensored marmot content" in "an act of desperation".

This content is family-friendly videos of the rodents scurrying around and popping out of their burrows, which so far has generated more than $5,000 (£3,712).

After OnlyFans takes its share, the UCLA-affiliated Rocky Mountain Biological Laboratory in Colorado will make about $4,000.

The Marmot Project, which has been running for more than 60 years, is the second-longest study of individually identified mammals in the world, after Jane Goodall's chimpanzee study in Tanzania.

It studies the yellow-bellied marmot, one of the 15 recognised species of marmot found in the Northern Hemisphere.

Because the species is neither threatened nor endangered, it helps scientists to understand the factors that drive population changes, according to the lab.

Blumstein said long-term studies such as these are really effective but, despite this, he has been unable to secure federal support.

While the lab will probably not be able to generate enough money through OnlyFans to save the project from spending cuts, he believes raising awareness about their work is also important.

The OnlyFans idea came to him when he sat in a meadow waiting for some marmots to pop out of the ground.

Blumstein had recently watched the TV show Margot's Got Money Troubles, where Elle Fanning's character starts an OnlyFans account to support herself as a single mother.

"Marmots' got money troubles," he thought to himself. "Maybe we should do something a little risqué".

He raised the idea with his lab students, and they came up with the name OnlyMarms. One student helped him set up the account.

That's when he hit a slight snag. He had to upload a photo of his driver's licence to verify his identity. But the platform flagged that he did not look like the account's profile photo of a marmot. A quick email exchange cleared the way for them to start posting videos.

Marmot content is posted on OnlyFans to raise money for scientific research

On OnlyMarms, users can see the Rocky Mountain marmots in their natural habitat. They aren't as social as their alpine counterparts, Blumstein said, and the female marmots get grumpier as they age.

In one video, a female marmot chases away a male who got too comfortable in her burrow. In another, a female is dubbed "the queen of the town" as she is caught on camera in the sun.

The lab doesn't give their subjects human-sounding names, in an effort to avoid bias in their research. Instead, they mark the rodents with dye and call them things like "dans_hat", "open_kite" and "Citroën".

The scientists have also launched Fat Marmot Week, styled after Fat Bear Week, where the public can vote for their favourite rotund rodent in a bracket-style tournament at the end of August. As hibernating animals, marmots put on weight before winter.

"It's fun to root for the chunkiest marmot, but behind the fun and games is a deathly serious competition against nature to pile on fat to survive the long, cold winter," Blumstein said in a press release announcing the tournament.

articles.title: One Night Only review – sex is legal for 12 hours a year in bizarre romcom
articles.summary: ‘What if The Purge was for premarital sex?’ is the odd, gimmicky elevator pitch for this slickly made yet ungainly oddity that can’t quite get past the grimness of its conceit Going into a romcom, there are always the same questions. Will there be genuine chemistry? Will the rom and the com be equal in parts? And, for the last decade and change, will this be the one that finally resurrects a genre long past its prime?
