articles.content:
‘What if The Purge was for premarital sex?’ is the odd, gimmicky elevator pitch for this slickly made yet ungainly oddity that can’t quite get past the grimness of its conceit

G oing into a romcom, there are always the same questions. Will there be genuine chemistry? Will the rom and the com be equal in parts? And, for the last decade and change, will this be the one that finally resurrects a genre long past its prime? But for Universal’s glossy late summer offering One Night Only , notably the first wide-releasing romcom since April , there are more probing questions than usual. The film is the ungainly result of a four-cocktails-in elevator pitch which imagines a world where single people are only legally allowed to have sex on one night of the year, an idea that has seen it been referred to as “Sex Purge”.

On paper, it’s the set-up for a grim Handmaid’s Tale -adjacent horror of a totalitarian state insisting extreme control over the body, but instead it’s used as the backdrop for a sunny meet-cute, screams of protest drowned out by a zippy Top 40 soundtrack. One sits down wondering not just if boy will end up with girl but also how the government would be able to enforce such tyranny and what horrifying punishments lay in store for those willing to pick personal freedom over state-mandated abstinence. If it sounds like far too much for a breezy summer romp to take on, then that’s because it most definitely is, an overstuffed yet undercooked soufflé that can’t quite, ahem, rise to the occasion …

Introductory text informs us, much to the baffled laughter of those at my screening, that “premarital sex has been outlawed in the US” and is now only legal for 12 hours on one night of the year. It’s a “government decreed sexual climate” where it’s now a “badge of honour” to be an incel, the result of what’s described as an “ideological grenade” thrown at Americans by Congress. People have been fitted with biosensors, which detect the chemicals released during sex, and they turn from red to green when one gets married or the sex purge begins, a night of debauchery and chaos as everyone desperately tries to find someone to couple up with (wouldn’t the other 364 days a year be used to plan this a little better?). Protection is mandatory (condom surge pricing goes all the way up to $2,000 apiece) and we’re briefly shown that the price to pay for breaking the law is severe (a poor older man is dragged into a police station for the crime of being horny).

New York City is where we spend that time, the natural setting for a film about both singledom and sex, and we follow the routes of Owen (Callum Turner) and Allie (recent Oscar nominee Monica Barbaro ) as they hunt for sex against a ticking clock. Owen had a plan with his girlfriend ( Maya Hawke ) but she chooses the night as an opportunity to hook up with a neighbour, while Allie is urged by her queer roommate, who calls it a night “for the straights”, to put on a revealing dress and get herself out there. Their paths intertwine and for reasons that never quite make sense, decide not to have sex with each other, and instead play wingman from Manhattan to Brooklyn and back again.

After the unforgivably unreal use of Glasgow as a junky replacement for New York in last week’s Spider-Man sequel (it often looked like it was set in a Broadway musical), one of the film’s biggest aces is its up-close and immersive on-location shooting. Director Will Gluck is a savvy commercial film-maker and there’s a bright and poppy slickness to how his film looks and moves, especially when compared with Netflix’s many murkily flat romcoms. But as with his last film, the surprise smash Anyone But You , he’s mastered the sleek aesthetic of a 2000s throwback but not much else. His leads here are a merciful improvement ( Sydney Sweeney and Glen Powell were among the most criminally vacant pairings we’ve ever seen in the genre), but again there’s not enough smart or specific writing, from kids’ TV writer Travis Braun, to justify why they wouldn’t just head to bed on first meet (yes, he’s vomited up two omakases near her feet but also, it’s sex purge night, guys!).

It’s less romcom and more an attempt to be a raunchy (if ultimately rather coy) sex caper as we go from scrape to scrape, involving ineffective and unfunny cameos (Julia Fox! Pete Davidson! Molly Ringwald! Nicholas Braun! Roma Maffia!) and a string of almost-shags. There’s a gimmicky, ADHD quality to the film and its many misfiring pop culture references, as if made to insist a gen Z audience away from their phones, and while I appreciated how this applied detail to the grabby production design (most scenes involve some sort of visual clue as to how the law has affected the day-to-day), it also felt like a distraction, a script made up of moments rather than a fully realised story. There’s no thought-through journey for our characters (he needs to plan less and she needs to sing more or something?) and while the attractively paired Turner and Barbaro are just about sturdy enough to convince us of the motions, their ho-hum banter is mostly too perfunctory to provoke us into caring about how they end up.

It might not surprise you where the story takes them but what did surprise me is how progressively sex-negative the film becomes, either ridiculing those who want it or applying a moral superiority to those who don’t.

There’s both too much yet not enough world-building here, enough questions answered to encourage us to ask 10 more (why does no one mention masturbation and wouldn’t that also trigger the biosensors?). It’s also just too unavoidably grim of a premise, especially at a dark political moment such as this, for us to ignore the ramifications or root for characters who aren’t trying to actively destroy such a barbaric system (what if Katniss just had fun during those Hunger Games?). Instead, One Night Only weirdly plays like lulling government propaganda, a film about sex purge to be released in time for sex purge that says that actually maybe sex purge is a good idea after all.

One Night Only is out in Australian cinemas on 6 August and in the US and the UK on 7 August

It might not surprise you where the story takes them but what did surprise me is how progressively sex-negative the film becomes, either ridiculing those who want it or applying a moral superiority to those who don’t.

There’s both too much yet not enough world-building here, enough questions answered to encourage us to ask 10 more (why does no one mention masturbation and wouldn’t that also trigger the biosensors?). It’s also just too unavoidably grim of a premise, especially at a dark political moment such as this, for us to ignore the ramifications or root for characters who aren’t trying to actively destroy such a barbaric system (what if Katniss just had fun during those Hunger Games?). Instead, One Night Only weirdly plays like lulling government propaganda, a film about sex purge to be released in time for sex purge that says that actually maybe sex purge is a good idea after all.
One Night Only is out in Australian cinemas on 6 August and in the US and the UK on 7 August

Formula One drivers are increasingly style icons, and though you wouldn’t find Charles LeClerc’s Puma racing shoes ideal for daily duty, the company’s street-friendly Speedcat offers much the same style. I’ve worn mine with everything from casual denim to dressier attire and found them comfortable enough for everyday usage. Yes, they make great driving shoes, too. Tim Stevens

This dress was the perfect choice for a recent trip to Spain, where I had to attend a really nice daytime event during a brutal heatwave. The little cutouts make it feel fancy, but the fabric is comfortable and cool. It pairs equally well with nice sandals, flats or chic white sneakers. Bernadette Machard de Gramont

My skin breaks out often (thanks, perimenopause) and daily cleansing with this electronic silicone brush is a game changer: it exfoliates more gently than many models, and unlike traditional brushes, doesn’t need replacement heads. My skin is smoother, clearer and healthier as a result. Julia Skinner

These socks are an everyday staple: they hold up to regular wear and are comfortable and the perfect height to go with sneakers and other low shoes. Added bonus: the tab at the back makes them less likely to ride down into your shoes. Julia Skinner

A lot of companies make ceramic nonstick cookware, and the coating will eventually wear out. The advantage of Made In’s is that underneath the coating you’re getting a high-quality tri-ply pan. It’s less a disposable nonstick pan and more a premium pan that happens to have a nonstick surface. Sal Vaglica

Unlike something like Made In cookware, where you’re paying for differences in materials and construction, cast iron is pretty straightforward – there’s not a huge performance advantage to spending significantly more on a premium French brand. So this Cuisinart performs just as well as options that cost twice as much, and it’s a great size for most meals serving four to five people. Sal Vaglica

These loafers were recommended by New York City-based lawyer Danica McBain in our guide to the best women’s shoes for the office. “I love them because they have zero break-in time and hug your feet the way ballet slippers do. I comfortably walk one mile to and from work in this pair. I recommend this shoe at every single chance I get,” she told us. If you’re building your autumn wardrobe, this rich espresso shade is now on sale for 35% off. Lauren Gould

These bowls are sturdier and better balanced than their cheaper counterparts, meaning less rust and a lower likelihood of tipping over. The grippy bottom keeps them from sliding, and a range of nest-able sizes means you always have what you need without taking up a ton of precious storage space. Julia Skinner

I’ve had these New Balance sneakers for a year or so and they’re really comfortable – not too squishy and not too firm, and ideal for my particular foot, which is flattish and wide. They come in a range of colors but I think the neutral colorway is best. Megan Reynolds

Many Dutch ovens are large and heavy, but this is the perfect size for smaller meals: think several servings of soup, or roasting a small piece of meat. Like all Le Crueset pans, it holds heat well and distributes it evenly, and moves from stove to oven to table effortlessly. Julia Skinner

When I don’t want to shell out over $100 for a candle, Voluspa is my go-to brand because it has great scents that are made with a clean-burning coconut and soy wax blend. This one comes in a nice embossed glass jar, and it smells fresh and citrusy without being cloying. Bernadette Machard de Gramont

These are on the expensive side, but I love Touchland’s scents, and they don’t dry my skin out the way other hand-sanitizing sprays do. They have a nice spraying mechanism, and I like that the packaging is very slim; they can be tucked into a pocket or any purse without being bulky. Bernadette Machard de Gramont

There’s a reason this is the brand so many pilots and flight crews use. It’s not the flashiest luggage and it’s not a hard-shell case, but it’s extremely well-built and a great value – especially for frequent and international travelers. Sal Vaglica

This is definitely a splurge, but if you love cold brew or nitro cold brew and don’t mind committing to proprietary capsules, it makes genuinely excellent coffee. Sal Vaglica

There’s nothing particularly technical about this sneaker, but that’s part of the appeal. It’s a classic that still has a little punk-rock edge compared with many of the more mainstream Nike and Adidas options. I also like the sale color options. Sal Vaglica

When we asked a serial world traveler for packing tips, she recommended Baboon to the Moon’s 32L duffle bag, which held a whopping three weeks’ worth of stuff on a trip to Australia. That duffle is currently sold out, but the similarly roomy 34L weekender bag is on sale for 41% off. Its light weight, TSA-friendly size and built-in shoe compartment make it a perfect travel buddy.

As per our testing, the beloved, leak-proof Owala FreeSip water bottle is more than just a pretty face: “For day-to-day use, the dual spout on the FreeSip is an outstanding perk,” said Filter contributor John Brandon. While that bottle is full price, the FreeSip twist is now 27% off.

After spending a month testing this popular styling tool against Shark’s FlexStyle we found that both delivered similar results. However, our writer, Juno DeMelo, noted that the Dyson felt and looked “more deluxe”. If you’re seeking a luxurious at-home style experience you can now grab Dyson’s Airwrap i.d. for over $100 off its original price.

I wear these unbelievably stretchy and soft Beyond Yoga leggings for just about everything: pilates, resistance training , napping and running errands and after my kid. So at this price of 33% off, I’m adding another color to cart because I can’t think of another pair in my rotation that delivers this same level of comfort and versatility.

Lauded as one of the top anti-ageing serums and night treatments that work hard on hydration while you sleep , Estée Lauder’s Advanced Night Repair is “loved by millions”, according to Guardian beauty columnist Sali Huges, and now 33% off. “Its silky, non-greasy texture contains the patented [Night Peptide], to soothe, tone and soften,” she said.

A college professor once recommended these 100% organic cotton Boll & Branch sheets as a dorm essential because they’re “like a warm hug that will lull you into your best sleep”. They’re now 30% off, and while they may fare particularly well in a dorm room for their cooling and comforting properties, we bet you’ll find their contrasting trim quite dreamy in your space too.

Without my trusty T3 one-step multi-styler, I’d be shelling out hundreds of dollars a month at the salon to tame my hair the “texture of a Brillo pad,” I said in my guide to the best gifts for new moms. Now 33% off, it’s your chance to embody serious mane character energy with its smoothing and defrizzing properties that don’t damage strands.

Parachute’s plush, organic cotton towel tops our list as the very best money can buy. “This bath towel feels like a luxury bathrobe,” said tester Jon Chan of the long-staple Turkish cotton towels boasting a thick and absorbent texture. Grab a similar model, this time with trendy ribbed details, for 34% off.

Le Creuset’s enamel cast-iron cookware embodies our ethos around buying “fewer, better things” with its nearly indestructible build, versatility across cuisines and cooking styles and a lifetime limited warranty that ensures a one-time investment. Outfit your kitchen with this 40%-off Dutch oven for the perfect sear on proteins or sumptuous stews for batch cooking.

We’re big fans of all things Our Place for its non-toxic, non-stick cookware that yielded restaurant-worthy cooking results in our tests. Try a little bit of everything for 33% off in this set including the mini and regular Always Pan 2.0 , the mini and regular Perfect Pot , a steamer basket and lids and beechwood utensils for each piece to facilitate stirring and serving.

The best time to stock up on new underwear you’ll need to buy on repeat anyway is a sale for 35% off. These gift-worthy and man-favorite Saxx boxer briefs offer chafe-free support, antimicrobial properties for freshness and a moisture-wicking fabric to stay cool and dry.

My Asics Nova Blast shoes have carried me through freezing pre-work runs and humid jogs through the streets of Manhattan. Their FF Blast Max cushioning make my feet feel like they’re bouncing on mini trampolines while the lightweight mesh upper makes them breathable enough for summer runs . You can snag them for 13% off in two stylish colorways (I especially like the black pearl pink ). Lauren Gould, Filter US editorial coordinator

If you prefer to stare at the world through rose-tinted lenses, be sure to jump on these trendy Ray-Ban specs for 38% off. The brand consistently tops the Filter’s best sunglasses lists for their ability to deviate from the ordinary while remaining sensible . Enjoy reliable 100% UV protection and a non-slip design that stays put in the face of sweat.

Our best-tested chef’s knife, now 28% off as part of a set with a serrated knife, is a buy-it-for-life treat. “This one ticks every single box,” said Filter reviewer, chef and kitchen expert Ben Lippett. “It feels fantastic in your hand, with a convincing, balanced heft that feels top quality.”

Packing light is a learned skill. Filter contributor Tobey Grumet Segal’s go-to luggage includes this now on-sale Beis hardshell carry-on that makes it second nature with its built-in pouches and omni-directional wheels for easy navigation. Make it yours in a glossy blue (that you’re unlikely to miss at baggage claim) for 25% off.

The Stokke Tripp Trapp convertible high chair grows with your child, lending it a family heirloom-like quality – now made all the more appealing with this 25% discount. For Guardian columnist Rhiannon Lucy Cosslett, the chair “has revolutionised how generations of children eat – a friend of mine says her family still sit on the ones she and her siblings had as babies.”

Our Place’s Wonder Oven Pro topped our air fryer tests. Now it’s on sale

Squishies and ‘a fuzzy book’: 21 things tweens want for back-to-school season, according to tweens

articles.title: ‘Getting old is no fun’: Game of Thrones author George RR Martin speaks out about depression amid further book delays
articles.summary: A new blog post by the fantasy writer has outlined his recent difficulties, as fans continue to speculate on the elusive sixth book in his A Song of Ice and Fire series George RR Martin has opened up about experiencing depression during a “stressful” and “overwhelming” year, as readers continue to await the long-delayed sixth instalment of his A Song of Ice and Fire series. The 77-year-old American author, whose fantasy novels shaped and inspired the hit HBO television series Game of Thrones, wrote candidly about his recent difficulties in his first personal blog post for almost six months. Continue reading...
articles.content:
A new blog post by the fantasy writer has outlined his recent difficulties, as fans continue to speculate on the elusive sixth book in his A Song of Ice and Fire series

George RR Martin has opened up about experiencing depression during a “stressful” and “overwhelming” year, as readers continue to await the long-delayed sixth instalment of his A Song of Ice and Fire series.

The 77-year-old American author, whose fantasy novels shaped and inspired the hit HBO television series Game of Thrones, wrote candidly about his recent difficulties in his first personal blog post for almost six months.

“This year has been … stressful, to say the least,” he wrote in a post titled Better Late Than Never . “So much has been happening, it’s been overwhelming. Some great things, exciting things. Dreams coming true. But there have been nightmares too. I have lost friends. Battled sadness and depression. The worst may be yet to come.”

He explained that posts published on his website since February had been written by his assistants because he had continued to fall behind despite their help.

Martin, who turns 78 in September, also reflected on ageing; “getting old is no fun”, he wrote, although he added that the year had contained “amazing times” alongside its difficulties.

“I suppose that’s just life. Of course, I knew that. If you’ve read my stories, you know that.”

Among the year’s highlights, Martin noted that A Knight of the Seven Kingdoms, HBO’s Game of Thrones prequel based on his Tales of Dunk and Egg novellas, had received nine Emmy nominations, including for outstanding drama series.

His comments come amid continued speculation about The Winds of Winter, the planned sixth and penultimate novel in A Song of Ice and Fire. The book has been in progress since the publication of the fifth instalment, A Dance with Dragons, in 2011, and has become one of the most eagerly awaited novels in modern publishing. No publication date has been announced.

Martin has faced sustained criticism from some readers over the delay, and has previously referred to the book as “the curse of my life”. The Game of Thrones TV show eventually overtook its source material, with its later seasons following a separate narrative that received a mixed response from critics and viewers, especially after its final season in 2019.

In a blog post in May 2025 , Martin directly addressed those who believed he had abandoned the series, sarcastically listing the accusations levelled against him: “I will never finish Winds. If I do, I will never finish A Dream of Spring. If I do, it won’t be any good.”

Continuing the charges, he wrote: “I am going to die soon anyway, because I am so old. I lost all interest in A Song of Ice and Fire decades ago. I don’t give a shit about writing any longer, I just sit around and spend my money.”

But Martin insisted that he remained invested in Westeros and its characters. “I care about them all,” he wrote. “More than you can ever imagine.”

In an interview with the Hollywood Reporter in January , Martin said he had completed about 1,100 manuscript pages of The Winds of Winter. He said leaving the series unfinished would feel like “a total failure”, adding: “I do think if I can just get some of these other things off my back, I could finish The Winds of Winter pretty soon … It’s been made clear to me that Winds is the priority, but … I don’t know. Sometimes I’m not in the mood for that.”

articles.content:
Our guest columnist reveals how he found his personal style, from jumpsuits to high-waisted trousers

O ther than the jumpsuits, I don’t think I wore anything particularly groundbreaking when I appeared on The Traitors . I just think the bar for men’s fashion is so low that for me to come on television in a chunky mint green jumper and a pair of high-waisted jeans – which is probably one of the most neutral looks I own – seemed like a revelation. There was no styling budget, so most of what I wore came from my wardrobe.

The discovery of my personal style began when I was at primary school on the Isle of Lewis, off the north-west coast of Scotland. I realised I was different to the other boys when I began experimenting with fashion. From a young age I was turning my hems up, and I was certainly more interested in what the girls in my class were wearing.

I would go so far as to say that my sexuality started to manifest in my choice of clothes. I have vivid memories of travelling to the mainland to go shopping – three hours on the ferry and then a 90-minute bus ride to Inverness. My biannual visit to Topman felt like a religious experience.

One of the first things I remember buying was a grey and black striped cardigan. It was just a simple cardigan, but when I wore it to school I got ripped to shreds. Boys did not wear cardigans then. I remember feeling disheartened that this thing that I loved so much – fashion – was bringing me so much distress.

By the time I was 16 or 17, it was becoming almost impossible to hide who I was. On another trip to the mainland I bought my first pair of skinny jeans, which were very fashion forward for the Isle of Lewis in the 00s. I never showed my skinnies to my parents. When I was going out with my friends in the evening, I would put them in a bag and change into them after leaving the house. I wish I had been able to see then that I was merely doing something that a lot of my straight male counterparts would be doing years later.

I went to the University of Glasgow when I was 18. Being in a city where everyone had access to all the same clothes meant I was no longer unique. That’s when I found vintage. (I was also a typical student with no money, and secondhand places were cheaper.) Everything on the high street was so flat, brown, beige, white, and I started seeing all these vintage Hawaiian shirts and incredible high-waist trousers. To me, the 60s, 70s and 80s were such a celebration of print and colour and drama. I can still remember loving this one pale blue 70s suit, but it was £50 – way out of my budget. Fifteen years on, I still wish I had bought it.

Once I figured out my look, I never looked back. It’s quite distinct, and I love that I can go to a party and never have to worry about someone wearing the same thing as me. I love vintage shirts with dagger collars or billowy sleeves, and vintage trousers that have a nice flare on them to add some drama. People called me Simon Cowell when I started wearing high waists, but I just think this is how I’m supposed to look.

The most stressful part of preparing to go on The Traitors had nothing to do with whether I would be a traitor or a faithful, or how far I’d get. It was: what the hell do I wear? I think people can ascertain so much about who you are through what you wear, it’s all snap judgments.

Having said that, it was never my goal to inspire an army of wide-legged trouser-wearing men; it was just to appear as the truest representation of myself. But since the show aired, I have had so many men message me on social media asking for clothes advice, and I’m going to use my next three columns to share my tips. So stay tuned for more, from tailoring to wedding dressing to – you guessed it – jumpsuits.

articles.title: Teachers need help with AI. A union is offering training – with $23m in funding from big tech
articles.summary: Partnership between American Federation of Teachers, one of the largest labor unions in the US, and AI firms has stirred controversy Darius Saczuk, a high school teacher, views artificial intelligence as his enemy. Earlier this year, he and several dozen New York City teachers spent the day inside a windowless conference room in downtown Manhattan to learn how to use AI and prevent students from outsourcing their thinking to it. As Saczuk sees it, he needs to understand his enemy in order to beat it. Continue reading...
articles.content:
Partnership between American Federation of Teachers, one of the largest labor unions in the US, and AI firms has stirred controversy

D arius Saczuk, a high school teacher, views artificial intelligence as his enemy. Earlier this year, he and several dozen New York City teachers spent the day inside a windowless conference room in downtown Manhattan to learn how to use AI and prevent students from outsourcing their thinking to it.

As Saczuk sees it, he needs to understand his enemy in order to beat it.

“It’s killing our jobs, it’s changing our society, it’s replacing humans,” said Saczuk, who teaches English as a new language at Long Island City high school in Queens. “In order to retain my job, I need to know how to use AI because it’s not going away.”

So he turned to training offered by the American Federation of Teachers, one of the largest labor unions in the US with roughly 1.8 million members, at its new National Academy for AI Instruction. Last year, the academy began offering in-person and virtual AI training across the country. The goal is to train 400,000 educators over the span of five years, helping them understand AI’s benefits and potential harms and also shape how it’s used in the classroom.

Without guidance from their schools or districts, many teachers are left to figure out whether and how to use AI tools. Though the AFT’s $23m training initiative is one of the few structured programs for teachers, its funding, provided entirely by Microsoft, OpenAI and Anthropic, is stirring controversy. Supporters say the training is necessary for the future, but critics argue the academy pushes AI into classrooms, steering teachers toward tools that undermine students’ learning.

“It’s handing more political power over” to big tech, said Audrey Watters, author of Teaching Machines: The History of Personalized Learning. It’s really “dangerous” for educators to partner with companies that “seem opposed” to the goal of education, she said.

AI has become a ubiquitous force in classrooms, despite the lack of official guidance. More than half of polled teens say they use AI for help with schoolwork and nearly six in 10 think using AI to cheat is a regular occurrence at their schools, according to a Pew Research Center survey conducted last fall. Meanwhile only about four in 10 teachers say their schools offer professional development or training related to AI, according to a recent NPR/Ipsos poll . And about half of all teachers polled say their school hasn’t offered any guidance on AI, or they’re unclear on what it is.

Teaching educators about AI is a “moral imperative”, said Randi Weingarten, the AFT president. She argues that AI training empowers teachers to make informed decisions about how, when or whether to use AI in their instruction. And without outside funding, it was a choice between taking big tech’s money or doing nothing, she said.

“There was no fairy godmother philanthropist that was sprinkling millions of dollars on us to actually create a mechanism to educate,” Weingarten said. “I am not promoting the use of AI. Educators need to know the tool.”

For Microsoft, which is contributing the largest share of funding at $12.5m, the goal is to give educators a voice in shaping how AI products are used, said Justin Spelhaug, leader of Microsoft’s education, workforce and nonprofit programs.

“By partnering with teachers’ unions … we believe we can learn directly from teachers on what they want and need in their classroom,” he said in a statement.

But Watters asserts that AI’s presence in the classroom is not a foregone conclusion.

“The industry would very much like us to believe that it’s not going away,” Watters said. “But the future is unwritten.”

Tech company leaders have largely painted AI as beneficial to education, some even claiming AI could replace teachers . But experts say there’s still a lack of research proving whether AI actually improves learning outcomes.

In a 2024 blog post , Sam Altman, the OpenAI CEO, said he envisioned a future where “children will have virtual tutors”. AI could replicate some of the meaningful experiences teachers provide, such as making students feel understood and inspired, Greg Brockman, the OpenAI president, said in 2023 on the Possible podcast , hosted by Reid Hoffman, the LinkedIn co-founder, and Aria Finger, his chief of staff.

“Imagine if you could give that kind of teacher to every student 24/7 … for free,” Brockman said.

Microsoft believes “AI can help reduce administrative burdens, personalize learning and create more time for students”, Spelhaug said. “But there is no substitute for the role of a teacher.”

OpenAI, which pledged $10m to the academy, and Anthropic, which committed $500,000 to the first year, did not respond to a request for comment.

AI companies are already making their way into classrooms. Over the last two years, Miami-Dade county public schools, one of the largest US districts, began rolling out Google’s Gemini chatbot to teachers and high school students . Last fall, Microsoft announced AI tools for teachers at no additional cost for educational customers. And OpenAI and Anthropic offer K-12 teachers free use of versions of their chatbots designed for educators.

There’s been a longstanding playbook in which tech companies provide free training and resources to teachers in exchange for feedback and product advocacy, said Justin Reich, a Massachusetts Institute of Technology professor and author of Failure to Disrupt: Why Technology Alone Can’t Transform Education.

Google, for example, entrenched itself in schools by offering districts free or low-cost educational software for classroom laptops. It’s also built a corps of Google Certified Educators, teachers trained on the company’s software who promote it to their peers. Last year, Google introduced free Gemini certifications for K-12 teachers and students as young as 13. But the aim is profits, Reich said.

“Their goal is to get people to become lifelong consumers,” he said. Still, “there’s no evidence that the adoption of Google or Microsoft products lead to better outcomes, happier teachers, more efficient school systems or anything”.

The AFT’s new academy seems to echo Google’s approach, Watters said. By offering training through a labor union, viewed as a peer group, tech companies make their AI products seem more credible, she said.

“It feels very different to have your union say, ‘We’re offering a training,’ than it does to have a company say [it],” Watters said.

“This initiative was designed in response to a need our union partners and educators themselves identified,” he said. “Our role is to provide resources and expertise while respecting the independence of the AFT and the professional judgment of teachers.”

The AFT doesn’t allow companies to promote products during the sessions, Weingarten said. And while she doesn’t think “students have to use AI in schools”, she believes educators cannot ignore what’s already here.

In a May speech at the National Press Club, Weingarten called for a ban on student-facing AI in elementary schools and said the AFT is working with Microsoft, OpenAI and Anthropic on a “gold standard” for AI safety and privacy in schools. If the companies don’t deliver on the promise, the union will walk away from the funding, she added.

“They have agreed in concept,” she said. “But until the Is are dotted and the Ts are crossed, there’s no agreement.”

Microsoft didn’t share any details or timeline about new standards, but Spelhaug said the company shares the AFT’s goal.

There’s no established approach for training teachers on AI. The technology is simply too new. But the academy’s leaders hope to work with teachers to find ways to use the technology without compromising students’ cognitive development, independent thinking, data privacy and mental health.

“The sad thing is there is no map, and the terrain is changing every single day,” John Holleran, an AI academy trainer said to teachers assembled at a May session. “So, it’s going to be difficult for us to sort of figure out where we’re going.”

Demand for the academy’s training is strong. A May training sold out within hours, leaving about 150 people on the waitlist, according to staff. The session focused on two key points: AI can’t replace teachers. And it can’t be blindly trusted because it can be biased or hallucinate, meaning make things up.

For example, ChatGPT generated an image of a white man in a suit and tie when asked to show a successful person – a bias Holleran said teachers need to be aware of when creating prompts.

Several teachers at the training said AI is already helping them tackle classroom challenges.

Phillip Perry, who teaches ninth grade at Bronx High School for Law and Community Service, uses AI to design lessons for students with disabilities.

“Trying to differentiate instruction in a way that can completely target their learning needs has been a massive challenge,” Perry said. “Using AI is helpful in breaking down tasks to the smallest form to help build the students up as they go.”

Tanushree Sengupta, a math teacher at Hillcrest high school in Queens, uses AI to generate practice math problems and, eventually, to analyze student data and flag those needing extra support or a challenge. But she worries that the tech could be a crutch.

“I need to figure out ways where [students are] doing more thinking that they can actually show,” she said, adding that she signed up for the training in part to help students think for themselves.

To that end, AFT trainers advised teachers to redesign their curriculum to favor student-led discussions, journaling and thought exercises that require human judgement and reasoning.

The training filled a void, offering practical strategies for the classroom, said Perry and Sengupta, who were unaware of the academy’s funding prior to speaking to the Guardian.

“As long as what they’re providing is beneficial to the students and the teachers, then I don’t see an issue,” Perry said.

Saczuk, the teacher from Queens, considered the training “necessary”. Still, he left with more questions than answers.

“What is the role of the teacher?” he asked. “It’s a big question mark.”

articles.content:
‘Looksmaxxing’ culture has led to the rise of facial analysis services – but experts warn they aren’t backed by science and can be harmful to users

Danielle, 37, didn’t always have issues with body image: she used to be a model and recalls receiving positive attention from men. However, when two years of unemployment plunged her into a period of financial insecurity, her confidence faded. “It was easy to wonder, if I was prettier, if some of my features were different, would that help?” she said.

So, when Danielle saw videos on TikTok about a “facial analysis” service that claimed it could provide her with “science-backed” glow-up advice, she bought it without hesitation. Three-hundred and thirty dollars later, after sending in selfies to be analyzed, Danielle received her personalized 30-page report from the company Qoves.

Qoves scored everything from Danielle’s ear shape to the femininity of her features. It recommended she get a rhinoplasty, a lower blepharoplasty , a canthopexy , chin implants and a malarplasty . Additionally: microblading, lash enhancements, filler in her temples and cheeks, a mixture of filler and Botox in her chin and jaw, and Botox around her mouth.

Danielle, who now works in tech in Colorado, is delaying any cosmetic surgery until she pays off the credit card debt accrued from her two years without a paycheck; once it is, she is interested in traveling to Mexico for procedures on her nose and eyelids. She also recently consulted a Botox and filler injector.

Qoves states that attractive people “get better treatment everywhere, from the hospital to the courtroom” and claims it is easier for them to find jobs and earn money. There is some truth to this: the “halo effect” is a documented phenomenon of good-looking people being perceived as smarter and more sociable than their average-looking counterparts, and studies have linked attractiveness to better pay . For Danielle, who asked to go by first name only for privacy, this promised material advantage was a selling point: “It gave me a motivation that I didn’t have in the past, which was seeing it as potentially helping my career and financial security.”

Plastic surgery and nonsurgical cosmetic enhancements such as Botox have unambiguously increased in popularity over the past two decades, to the point that the aesthetics of bought beauty have become inescapable on social media. This has opened the door for “looksmaxxing” influencers , who take fixation with appearance to the extreme. Coalescing around the language of science and “self-improvement”, looksmaxxers claim that attractiveness can be quantified – that individual features should be analyzed and empirically scored, and physical improvements are made where necessary. The ultimate goal is to achieve “facial harmony”, or the ideal proportions of nose, eyes and other features in relationship to one another.

“I do believe that the standard I’ve acquired for what’s beautiful is impossible to achieve without spending thousands of dollars,” Danielle said, noting that her confidence decreased when she started using TikTok. “All of the people that I look at [on social media] and think are beautiful have gotten plastic surgery.”

Océane, who lives in France, paid an additional $80 for express delivery and received her results from Qoves in two days. It provided her a sense of relief: the report didn’t recommend any changes to her nose and otherwise “confirmed what I already knew about my flaws”, she said.

Dr Tracy Vaillancourt is a professor of psychology at the University of Ottawa and one of the many scholars Qoves cites in promotional materials. She expressed concern about the negative psychological impact of facial analysis services on self-esteem. “This is what women are most insecure about: their appearance,” she said. “There are going to be some who are told they look better than they thought and that’s great. Is that really going to be sustained over time?” In other words, can a service that emphasizes appearance as a metric of self-worth ever provide someone with lasting peace of mind, or does it perpetuate a cycle of self-criticism?

Moreover, though Qoves and Epica limit their services to adults aged 18 and up, the age restrictions are easy for minors to bypass. Qoves users are expected to self-report issues with self-image, with few guardrails in place to deter anyone with body dysmorphia disorder before they are presented with a menu of their flaws. “You can circumvent that so easily, it’s just going to give them the appearance of due diligence and making sure they’re not exploiting people who are vulnerable – but ultimately, they will be exploiting people who are vulnerable,” Vaillaincourt said. “These sorts of things are so destructive to people who have body dysmorphia, dysphoria, a history of eating disorders and people with low self-esteem.”

Qoves referenced Vaillancourt’s work in a video called The Cost of Being Too Pretty to show that beautiful women face jealousy from others. But Vaillancourt isn’t a scholar of beauty: she researches bullying, mental health and violence prevention. Though Qoves correctly interpreted her research on physical appearance and hostility, she is uneasy about research like hers being used for paid services like Qoves, that she believes have the capacity to harm women’s mental health.

Beyond Vaillancourt’s research, the applications of “science” used to back up these facial analysis services are shaky at best.

Qoves breaks down customers’ features based on “masculine and feminine facial qualities”, it explains in a video referencing a 2018 bulletin in the journal Frontiers of Psychology. Dr Justin Mogilski, psychology professor at the University of South Carolina Salkehatchie, co-authored the bulletin. However, his research was a limited view of how a group of primarily college-aged Americans perceived certain features as masculine or feminine.

“Do findings like mine generalize to every single population that makes up the world or a country? Or within every context where the attractiveness of a given feature can vary based on local ecology or culture? They do not,” Mogilski said. “So, would I make suggestions [for facial enhancements] based on our or anyone else’s data? I would not.”

Some services do not make any pretense of considering location or cultural standards in how they quantify beauty. On its website, Epica reports a commitment to diversity and inclusion, though it is unclear how its methodology reflects this – particularly as AI tools are increasingly criticized for perpetuating racial bias. Qoves insists its analyses are appropriate for all ethnicities, and says it will “consider unique facial traits and characteristics common to your demographic” when creating a report. In reality, as some people have pointed out online, its promotional materials often replicate Eurocentric conceptions of beauty: slim noses and large, double-lidded eyes for women, for example. As one person commented on a Qoves video breaking down Bangladeshi women’s faces: “What’s shown here seems to reflect a beauty ideal rather than the real diversity of Bangladeshi women.”

The lack of transparency around the methods and metrics the services use to measure attractiveness is its own issue. “These services owe it to their clients and themselves – if they want to be seen as credible – to be able to demonstrate scientifically” what their methods are, said Dr Mitch Brown, an assistant professor of psychological science at the University of Arkansas who has studied the science of attraction for over a decade. According to experts such as Brown, the available literature on attractiveness is too heterogenous, making any universal, population-wide generalizations questionable. And, even if we know certain features are deemed as attractive by a specific community, are these findings lasting enough to justify changing one’s appearance? Are they sound enough to support a paid service’s recommendation?

“I don’t think the science is anywhere clear enough to do that. I would caution anyone against that,” Brown said.

In an email to the Guardian, Epic said: “We are unable to disclose proprietary information regarding our algorithmic methodologies, technical frameworks, or internal product development details.” It continued: “We continually review and refine our platform to ensure our services provide a supportive, fair and positive experience for all users.”

I purchased my own report with Qoves and uploaded my selfies to Epica to see what these tools really offered.

For Qoves, I was asked to check boxes confirming that I did not have “concerns related to body dysmorphic disorder” and would be comfortable receiving weight loss recommendations, and then asked to upload pictures of my face and side profile.

A couple of days later, Qoves presented me with an 18-tab analysis of each of my features, along with a 16-page “aesthetic protocol”, complete with a disturbing mockup of what my face would look like should I implement its recommendations: a healthy dose of lip filler, makeup and the overly tweezed eyebrows I sported in 10th grade.

For Epica, I was asked: how often do I use makeup? Do I want more control over my appearance? Instantly, I received a “skin health” score of 61%, with uneven texture highlighted as the main concern and a flood of serums advertised across my screen to fix it. I then moved to my couch, retook a selfie in the new lighting, and saw my skin health score jump to 81%.

Before receiving these reports, I had never considered whether my mouth was upturned or wide, or whether or not Botox at my ripe age of 26 would be beneficial. I had not considered “dark feminine” makeup styles as being my look. But now I found myself second-guessing what I saw in the mirror. Just how downturned did my mouth really look to those around me? How would Botox or a haul of new makeup change features I hadn’t previously been concerned about?

“Ultimately, there are going to be implications for mental health,” Vaillancourt said, “and it’s going to be about social comparison: never feeling good enough, never achieving enough.”

articles.content:
Set on an idyllic Canadian island, this coming-of-age series is juicy stuff. It swaps the darkness of recent YA TV for warmth, humour and a surprisingly compelling mystery

I ’ll be honest: I was prepared to grit my teeth through Sterling Point, Prime Video’s newest coming-of-age offering, which I dismissed as another by-the-numbers high-school drama. The show follows a type-A teen on a journey of sun-dappled self-discovery, escaping her native New York for an idyllic getaway on a picturesque Canadian island. It’s an unassuming, summer camp-style narrative, but in the style of last year’s seasonal phenomenon that was series three of The Summer I Turned Pretty , it manages to transcend the limits of its YA niche, revealing itself to be quite juicy.

Protagonist Annie (Ella Rubin) is a highly strung 17-year-old, still reeling from a rejection from a summer business school programme when she receives the news that her estranged maternal grandfather has left her some mysterious assets. Annie, whose mother had died years ago, and her twin Connor (Keen Ruffalo), are prompted to start digging through family secrets, much to the distress of their dad (Jay Duplass of Transparent and Industry). The two learn that they’ve inherited a house in Canada – prompting Annie to take off on a secret trip in search of answers about her late mother’s life.

We find ourselves on Sterling Point where Annie quickly finds herself a group of free-spirited friends, including Oona (Bo Bragason), the carefree and sexually forward linchpin of the group; Ellis (Jacob Whiteduck-Lavoie), the cheeky local who flies Annie out to the island on a precarious seaplane; Rory (Daniel Quinn-Toye), a sensitive New Yorker who gets compared to Timothée Chalamet; and Ramona (Amélie Elisabeth Hoeferle), who drops a bombshell at the end of the show’s first episode. It rapidly becomes clear that the group is going to spend their leisurely time swimming in beautiful lakes, boating and crushing on each other.

Beyond an intriguing central plot full of familial mysteries – which I can’t go into without entirely spoiling things – the show is doing something interesting in its generational context. Unlike the sort of timeless, placeless high-schoolers that millennial-plus screenwriters often dream up, these gen Z and gen alpha characters (from the creators of My Old Ass and Gossip Girl) talk like actual young people, and reflect their modern preoccupations.

Among this crew, there’s lots of fluidity, and an overflow of emotional literacy. Oona’s little sister, Maple (Mabel Strachan), is casually reading Bessel van der Kolk’s The Body Keeps the Score : “I need to find out what the score is, and where in the body it’s being kept.” The sexualities of many of the characters are a sort of question mark, slowly emerging or shifting as the show goes on, reminiscent of coming-of-age forebears such as The Half of It and Booksmart . No one’s gender or queerness is turned into a major plot point, reflecting the fact that more than one in five gen Zs identify as LGBTQ+ . I laughed out loud at a quip about Oona, who, like her own mother, has repeated noncommittal flings that don’t turn into anything serious. “So she’s avoidant attached? We can work through that,” says 17-year-old Connor.

The bounds of the YA genre, and of television, feel pretty flexible here. Lines get blundered a few times, and the cameras keep rolling – since the young actors were explicitly encouraged to improvise on set. There are moments where this can fall a bit flat: a punchline doesn’t quite land, or you experience the metaphorical emotional equivalent of seeing a boom in shot. But this also allows for a looser, more authentic feel. The plot and pacing take the same approach – in the spirit of Duplass’s Transparent , sometimes a plotline gets teed up and then completely disappears, subverting the usual rules of television and making things feel more frenetic.

Again, there are drawbacks to this approach. More than once, the show contains what feels like a glaring plot hole. But the strangeness of these plotting and script flourishes creates an electricity that is actually more interesting than the love triangles, paternity secrets and other age-old devices at play here.

In April, season three of the once boundary-pushing teen drama Euphoria was met with flop reviews . The darkness that had once distinguished and sustained the show had spiralled out of control into a nightmarish, violent and hallucinatory sex fest. The show’s first season, much like Skins, upended the glossy, sanitised teen TV of the 2010s, giving us something that felt gritty and real. Perhaps now we’re seeking an escape from this. “You turn on Netflix and it’s, like, One Tree Hill and Gossip Girl. They’re all trending again,” Canadian creator Megan Park recently told Teen Vogue .

This feeling of refuge is enhanced by the fact that phones and social media barely feature in the show, despite the fact that teenagers now average more than eight hours of screen time per day . Technology is swapped for the ambient sounds and textures of nature, as well as real-life conversation, with all of its accompanying miscommunications and deceptions.

If escapism is the brief, then Sterling Point fulfils it expertly. Sure, it doesn’t carry the intensity or the existentialism of its edgier counterparts. But I was surprised by how long I wanted to stay with these characters and inhabit their island bubble. It kept subverting my expectations. I didn’t want to go home.

The plot and pacing take the same approach – in the spirit of Duplass’s Transparent , sometimes a plotline gets teed up and then completely disappears, subverting the usual rules of television and making things feel more frenetic.

Again, there are drawbacks to this approach. More than once, the show contains what feels like a glaring plot hole. But the strangeness of these plotting and script flourishes creates an electricity that is actually more interesting than the love triangles, paternity secrets and other age-old devices at play here.

In April, season three of the once boundary-pushing teen drama Euphoria was met with flop reviews . The darkness that had once distinguished and sustained the show had spiralled out of control into a nightmarish, violent and hallucinatory sex fest. The show’s first season, much like Skins, upended the glossy, sanitised teen TV of the 2010s, giving us something that felt gritty and real. Perhaps now we’re seeking an escape from this. “You turn on Netflix and it’s, like, One Tree Hill and Gossip Girl. They’re all trending again,” Canadian creator Megan Park recently told Teen Vogue .

This feeling of refuge is enhanced by the fact that phones and social media barely feature in the show, despite the fact that teenagers now average more than eight hours of screen time per day . Technology is swapped for the ambient sounds and textures of nature, as well as real-life conversation, with all of its accompanying miscommunications and deceptions.

If escapism is the brief, then Sterling Point fulfils it expertly. Sure, it doesn’t carry the intensity or the existentialism of its edgier counterparts. But I was surprised by how long I wanted to stay with these characters and inhabit their island bubble. It kept subverting my expectations. I didn’t want to go home.

articles.title: ‘I put a raging dent in Neil Young’s forehead!’ Tim Pope on his riotous videos for the Cure, Bowie, Queen, Soft Cell and more
articles.summary: He dressed Freddie Mercury as a prawn, got Paul Weller to wear lipstick, put a camera in Robert Smith’s mouth and created a 75ft penis for Hall & Oates. articles.content:
He dressed Freddie Mercury as a prawn, got Paul Weller to wear lipstick, put a camera in Robert Smith’s mouth and created a 75ft penis for Hall & Oates. Pope looks back on is wild adventures with titans of music

A s video director to the stars in the golden age of MTV , Tim Pope’s trademark was putting his very famous clients in uncomfortable or dangerous situations. He dressed Freddie Mercury as a “giant Mediterranean prawn”, locked the Cure in a flooded wardrobe then chucked it off a cliff, and almost electrocuted two Psychedelic Furs.

“The core of my work seems to be sadism,” he chuckles. “I have wondered if it was all some sort of revenge for the brutality I suffered away at primary school, but maybe I’m just cruel.”

Whichever, it hasn’t served him badly. Pope’s glittering client list included megastars such as David Bowie and Paul McCartney, most of whom were only too willing to be – almost literally – tortured for their art. In the foreword for I Shoot Rock Stars, Pope’s riotous new memoir, the Cure’s Robert Smith sings the praises of “every moment” in his company “apart from the hours spent drowning in freezing filthy water, being asphyxiated by snakes, slowly being fed into a giant spider’s mouth, cut off at the knees, being chucked off a pier or orally endoscoped”.

“That was for the video for Lullaby ,” sniggers Pope, now a youthful 70-year-old with a mischievous grin. “I had to run a camera inside Smithy’s mouth at risk of knocking out his sweet little teeth.”

Bowie, who Pope worked with in the 80s and 90s, was similarly trusting. “I strapped a camera to him and got him to fall forward,” explains the film-maker. “If he’d have fallen in the wrong way it would probably have impaled him.”

In fact, Pope started his memoir after coming across a years-old answerphone message from the singer, who died in 2016. “It was like David was speaking to me from beyond the grave, because I never said goodbye to him,” he says. “I realised I’d been around all these amazing things.”

Pope’s wild ride began at Latymer Grammar School in Enfield, London, where the new film studies class introduced him to directors such as Alfred Hitchcock and Roman Polanski and “the concept of the auteur”. Funding his new hobby by doing a paper round and working in a chip shop, soon enough he smuggled his first 8mm film camera into an Emerson, Lake and Palmer concert: “Down my trousers, at immense pain to myself.”

After film college, he was working at a company training politicians to appear on TV when he started moonlighting for record labels, filming bands playing live for £100 a pop. There were very few video directors then, and the world of David Mallet (Blondie, Bowie, Queen) or Russell Mulcahy (Duran Duran, Elton John) felt like “an impenetrable club”. Then Soft Cell had a global smash with Tainted Love and hurriedly needed a video for the follow-up, Bedsitter . “I’d met this art director, Al McDowell, who went on to work with Spielberg,” explains Pope. “We came up with mad ideas, drew up a storyboard and after the video was shown on Top of the Pops the floodgates opened.”

Pope’s emergence coincided with MTV’s 1981 launch as a global music video platform. However, he rejected what he calls their “thou shalts” – “Thou shalt make your stars wear Spandex”, “Thou shalt include babes with big hair and even bigger boobs”, etc – in favour of what he calls: “Defiant individualism. Rebellion was in my DNA. I wanted to cause trouble.”

He filmed Soft Cell amid chains, raw meat and maggots for Sex Dwarf, after which the police confiscated the film. After the Style Council’s Long Hot Summer video showed Paul Weller playfully stroking bandmate Mick Talbot’s ear, the singer’s father/manager John phoned up asking: “What are you doing with my boy?” “For another video Paul came out wearing lipstick,” Pope remembers. “I think he was rebelling against norms and the image people had of him.”

Rather than adopt the off-the-peg style of many of his peers, Pope saw himself as a “bespoke tailor”, personalising each video to the song and artist. He made 37 of them for the Cure. Because Close to Me drew on Smith’s childhood claustrophobia when he was bedridden with chickenpox, Pope put the band in a wardrobe. For The Lovecats , he came across the ideal location in an estate agent’s window. “They let me view the house and gave me the keys,” he sniggers. “Next thing I know, I’m in there with the crew. Smithy and the boys piling out of the van. The neighbours must have heard The Lovecats coming through the walls.” Pope handed back the keys and the clandestinely shot video went around the world.

Pope’s regular clients were as maverick or uncompromising as he was. He filmed the The videos underneath a steam train and in a Spanish Harlem brothel and blasted Talk Talk’s Mark Hollis with an aircraft engine. Pope drew on Neil Young’s “emotionally raw real-life personality” for a succession of fictional characters – psychotic old drifters or, in Pressure, the guy who punches himself so hard he actually knocks himself out. Once, filming closely, Pope’s camera left the star with a “raging dent in his forehead like a third eye. But I got this amazing shot past his nose on to the keyboard.”

He freely admits a “Spinal Tap period”: a 75ft penis on wheels for Hall and Oates, or Queen’s It’s a Hard Life “prawn” costume video, which led drummer Roger Taylor to comment: “No artist has ever looked as silly in a video.” By the late 80s, Pope was “jetting about on Concorde, hanging out with Iggy Pop …” The chapter Iggy’s “Cock” Moment describes the time his camera captured the rocker’s exposed “schlong” on stage. Pope writes about his adventures like he talks, in mild disbelief: “Lou fucking Reed and David fucking Bowie, and me, a boy from Enfield, trying to play it cool.”

He’d met Bowie when Iggy said he’d invited “a couple of mates” who turned out to be the superstar and Mick Jagger. Then, at Bowie’s Wembley concert, the singer introduced him to Princess Diana. “Sitting behind her while she was hand jiving and singing ‘Time flexes like a whore’ along with Bowie was a brilliant moment,” Pope smiles, “but I got glimpses of the real people. David fretting about his son’s exam results. Freddie making me cups of tea and calling them ‘Matildas’. Behind the gossamer artifice of fame they’re just human beings.” He writes movingly of his friendship with the usually enigmatic Mark Hollis, and their blissful hours spent laid flat, “letting music wash over us. ‘Fancy some fuckin’ Satie, Pope-ay?’ ‘More sherr-ay, Pope-ay?’”

In the 90s, after his short film, Phone , won various awards, Martin Scorsese wrote to him saying he liked it and Pope found himself being “seduced, in a way” by Hollywood. Specifically, he was recruited by the now imprisoned Harvey Weinstein to direct the sequel to The Crow. “A movie which made a lot of money but in which a young man, Brandon Lee, had died. So it was a tricky situation: but I’d loved Reservoir Dogs and Pulp Fiction. This was before we knew about wanking into flowerpots and destroying women’s lives.

“He was still seen as ‘good old Harvey’, the most powerful man in Hollywood, but his other nickname was Harvey Scissorhands. He had a reputation for meddling in the cutting room and I suffered that really badly. I poured everything into that film and ended up with something I loathed, and he said the worst three words anyone ever said to me: ‘We own you.’ Cos they did at that point.” The book doesn’t flinch from what he calls “a brutal experience”, after which Pope returned to London, didn’t make another video for 12 years or a film for 25. He says he carries “mental scars” to this day.

Pope argues that the golden age of video ended when MTV dropped “Music Television” from its logo in 2010, but he still makes videos and is currently casting a film called The Photographer’s Assistant as well as putting together a 50th-anniversary documentary about the Cure.

“I’ve read that my work has been viewed a trillion times, but I’m just a music fanboy from north London who got to work with most of his heroes,” he says. But he does have one more ambition: “I hope Harvey Weinstein reads my book.”

articles.title: Apple issues new challenge against UK order for access to private user data
articles.summary: It is the latest development in the ongoing dispute between Apple and the Home Office over data privacy.
articles.content:
Apple has confirmed it has launched a new legal complaint against the UK government at a court that deals with objections to the use of covert surveillance powers.

The tech giant has not told BBC News what the complaint relates to but the Financial Times , external has reported it is another challenge to a Home Office demand for so-called "backdoor" access to highly encrypted Apple user data.

The row, which centres on the government's desire to be able to see material protected by an advanced data protection system - which currently even Apple itself cannot access - has been rumbling on since early 2025.

The government said it would not comment on legal proceedings or what it called "operational matters".

But it added in a statement: "The UK supports strong encryption and robust privacy protections, but it is also vital that law enforcement can access communications when necessary and proportionate to protect the public from terrorism, serious crime, and child sexual abuse."

Apple has meanwhile referred reporters to a statement given last year, after its initial challenge to the UK government's request .

This said it was "gravely disappointed" it could still not offer its Advanced Data Protection feature to new UK users, following its decision to withdraw it in February 2025.

"As we have said many times before, we have never built a backdoor or master key to any of our products or services and we never will," the company added.

Since last February, UK iPhone users have been met with a notice on the Advanced Data Protection settings page which says the tool cannot be enabled.

Advanced Data Protection is an opt-in feature that allows users to turn on a higher level of protection for data stored in iCloud, such as back-ups, Drive storage, photos and voice memos.

It is secured using end-to-end encryption - meaning not even Apple would be able to see its contents.

The government's requests for Apple to permit it access to data held under this system were issued under the Investigatory Powers Act (IPA).

It includes powers allowing the government to issue secret notices - called technical capability notices - which can secretly force companies to provide UK security services with ways to access customer data.

The government had fought unsuccessfully to keep legal challenges to its first notice to Apple secret.

Its notice was later withdrawn after angering US politicians, who were concerned it would affect their own citizen's data.

But the government issued a new request in October which did not apply to US users .

Privacy groups which previously campaigned against its secret orders welcomed Apple's new legal complaint.

"We are happy to learn that Apple is once again challenging the UK's regime of secret orders," said Privacy International.

"While we don't know the substance of Apple's claim, if it relates to the previously reported orders aimed at undermining the security of Apple's iCloud storage, then Apple's claim, alongside side ours and Liberty's, is crucially important to preserving all of our privacy and security."

Ruth Ehrlich, director of external relations at Liberty, said the case was "hugely important" and has "far-reaching implications for the public's privacy rights well into the future".

"End-to-end encryption is an essential security tool that protects our personal data, including our bank details, health information, private conversations and images," she said.

"Opening a backdoor to all of that information carries a wide range of risks to our personal data. It is critical that the Government listens to the many concerns and commits to protecting our privacy rights."

But Sir Brian Leveson, the Investigatory Powers Commissioner, who provides independent oversight of the use of surveillance powers, has previously criticised media use of the term "backdoor" , external .

He said notices such as those concerned in this case would only be issued "if the Secretary of State deems it necessary and proportionate, and this decision is independently reviewed and approved by a Judicial Commissioner".

He added requests for data would also require separate authorisation under the IPA and these would be subject to independent oversight.

articles.content:
Decision to stage solo exhibition comes 15 years after conviction over racist and antisemitic remarks

The controversial designer John Galliano is to get an unvarnished retrospective at the Metropolitan Museum of Art’s Costume Institute in New York next May.

Galliano, who is widely considered to be one of the most influential designers of the past four decades, was exiled from the industry in 2011 after he was filmed making a series of racist and antisemitic comments. He was fired from his position as creative director of Dior, a post he had held for 15 years, condemned by the media and later convicted and fined by a French court.

At the time it was questioned whether the British designer would ever be able to redeem himself in the fashion industry.

The decision by the Met to spotlight Galliano with his own fashion blockbuster, which will be only the third time it has given a living designer a solo exhibition, suggests that perhaps, he has reached the pinnacle of his rehabilitation. The exhibition will be kicked off by the annual Met Gala red carpet extravaganza, making it one of the biggest events on the fashion calendar.

“The fashion business has a short memory,” said Dana Thomas, the author of Gods and Kings: The Rise and Fall of Alexander McQueen and John Galliano. “It is also remarkably forgiving of bad behaviours.”

Olya Kuryshchuk, the founder and editor in chief of the platform 1 Granary , described it as “refreshing” to see the celebration of a living artist rather than a typical thematic exhibition.

“Few designers have left a mark on fashion as profound as John Galliano,” she said. “He fundamentally changed the way fashion communicates emotion, fantasy and storytelling and influenced generations of designers.”

Thomas describes Galliano as having “worked hard to earn the industry’s forgiveness”. A documentary in 2024 by Kevin Macdonald delved into this redemption as the designer recalled how he spent time in rehabilitation for alcohol addiction and met prominent Jewish leaders to seek forgiveness. Within three years of his outburst, Galliano was appointed the creative director of Maison Margiela, a post he held for a decade and where he was widely lauded.

Since then his reintegration into the fashion industry has stepped up even further. In January, he sat front row at Jonathan Anderson’s debut show for Dior. In March, it was announced Galliano was embarking on a “two-year creative partnership” with Zara on a series of collections, the first of which hits stores in September.

According to the New York Times, the Met has held several meetings with Jewish leaders over the past year to discuss the event. In May, the Costume Institute’s head curator, Andrew Bolton, Vogue’s global editorial director and Met trustee, Anna Wintour, along with Galliano, attended a closed-door meeting met “a handful of the most influential rabbis and Jewish leaders in New York City”.

According to a press release, the exhibition, which is split into three parts, “will address the derogatory conduct that fundamentally altered his career and public reception. In doing so, the exhibition will consider how artistic achievement should be understood alongside ethical accountability.”

Wintour has championed Galliano since his graduate collection show at Central Saint Martins in London in 1984. She helped him secure financial support for his collections including his breakthrough spring-summer 1994 Paris show, which featured Kate Moss as a runaway bride, and championed him for roles at Givenchy and Dior. Insiders said a Met exhibition was originally planned for 2024 but was postponed after some board members voiced concerns.

Writing on Vogue.com Wintour said: “There is no one more deserving of an exhibition of this scale than John Galliano. He’s a great designer and his career isn’t defined by a moment – something that he will live with for the rest of his life. The exhibition won’t shy away from any of the darkness in John’s past. It’s part of what has shaped him. The show will take in the full arc of his career and grapple with all of it.”

The exhibition John Galliano: Horizons will feature garments, accessories, sketches and research books with the aim of revealing “how Galliano brings places, histories, artistic traditions, narratives, and identities into unexpected relation and transforms these encounters into imaginative garments”.

As the Costume Institute is the holder of the largest collection of Galliano’s work in the world, the exhibition is expected to include pieces from his earliest collections alongside examples from his more recent tenures.

Bolton said the exhibition would trace “how images become ideas, ideas become material, and material becomes emotion”. It would also explore “both how Galliano has remapped the world through fashion and how his conduct, its consequences, and changing cultural values have reshaped our understanding of his work”, Bolton added.

The show will begin by showing how Galliano’s collections relate to broader cultural events. The museum said this was where the exhibition would “directly address the rupture caused by his antisemitic, racist, and anti-Asian conduct in 2010 and 2011”.

However, rather than “presenting a conventional narrative of disgrace and redemption, the gallery will examine how memory, experience, cultural values, and historical circumstances continually reshape the reception of a designer’s work. It will invite visitors to consider how aesthetic achievement, ethical accountability, and institutional recognition intersect.”

Sarah Gresty, the course leader of the fashion BA at Central Saint Martins, said Galliano was still an inspiration for many of its students. “Lots of students admire the skill and aesthetic ambition of Galliano so I am not surprised by the news. The museum obviously have decided his work merits that platform.”

Thomas added that the retrospective would show whether the public had forgiven Galliano too, or whether “extraordinary talent” ultimately outweighed even “extraordinary transgressions”.

articles.title: World Cup 2026: England frustrated; Scotland face Brazil; Infantino defends hydration breaks – live
